name: Big Pocono State Park
why: Summit park on Camelback Mountain with three-state views; DCNR warns the steep access road should not be attempted with a trailer in tow.

name: Tobyhanna State Park
why: A 170-acre lake at nearly 2,000 ft with a 135-site modern campground and an RV sanitary dump station.
rigNote: Used the feed's max TRAILER length (45ft), not its max RV length (65ft), because the 65 is inconsistent with everything else on the record and looks like a group/organized-area artifact - flagging the conflict rather than reporting 65. Campendium independently lists the park max at 45ft. 136 sites: 26 with 50-amp electric, 104 non-electric; NO pull-throughs, all back-in; no water or sewer at sites. Campendium's longest reported rig is 33ft; that camper's 33ft Class A with 3 slides had 'a good size' fairly level site, but another warns sites are hard to back into 'due to the angle of the road and trees' and that the Pocono terrain means heavy leveling. Realistic for the coach only on a pre-selected 50-amp site.

name: Gouldsboro State Park
why: Quiet 250-acre Gouldsboro Lake, managed with Tobyhanna and popular for fishing and paddling.

name: Promised Land State Park
why: Two Pocono Plateau lakes ringed by Delaware State Forest, with 390+ campsites including full-hookup sites at Pickerel Point.
rigNote: DELIBERATELY NOT using the reservation number. The PA feed reports a 130ft max RV length against a 35ft max TRAILER length and a big-rig flag of NO - a 95ft gap that can only be a group-area artifact, and pulling the agency site list confirms real driveways of 25/30/35ft Back-In (sites 317, 318, 328). Campendium's park max of 45ft is the credible figure and is corroborated by a camper who actually stayed with a 40ft Class A ('Roads are in bad shape. The sites are fine') and a 35ft fifth wheel whose 'pull-through site was more than ample'. 392 sites over six areas; full-hookup sites exist at Pickerel Point, which is where a 40ft coach would have to go. Multiple reviewers flag poor internal road condition.

name: Hickory Run State Park
why: Boulder Field, a National Natural Landmark, plus 40+ miles of trail and a large campground with some full-hookup sites.
rigNote: Feed gives 40ft max RV / 40ft max trailer - the two agree, so 40 is a real ceiling, not an artifact - across 385 sites with a mix of tent-only, non-electric, electric and FULL-HOOKUP (water/sewer/electric). Pull-throughs available, but big-rig flag is NO. Campendium also caps it at 40ft with a longest reported rig of 37ft. Approach on PA-534 has a short ~14% grade and a switchback at River Rd, both reported as manageable by 35ft and 37ft fifth wheels. Exact 40ft fit for the coach - book a full-hookup pull-through and drop the toad.

name: Beltzville State Park
why: A 949-acre lake with a big sand beach and boat launches; overnight stays of any kind are prohibited.

name: Lehigh Gorge State Park
why: A deep, steep-walled river gorge with whitewater releases and a rail-trail on the old railroad grade.

name: Nockamixon State Park
why: The 1,450-acre Lake Nockamixon for sailing and fishing, with cabins and disc golf but no tent/RV campground.

name: Jacobsburg Environmental Education Center
why: Historic Henry gun-works site with creekside and ridge trails along Bushkill Creek; day use only.

name: Nescopeck State Park
why: Wetlands and rich forest habitat along Nescopeck Creek between Nescopeck and Mount Yeager; day use only.

name: Frances Slocum State Park
why: A horseshoe-shaped 165-acre lake with a 100-site campground, 85 of them tent-or-trailer sites with some electric.

name: Lackawanna State Park
why: A 198-acre lake with forested electric-hookup campsites, yurts and cottages north of Scranton.

name: Delaware State Forest
why: The forest wrapping the Poconos, with 29 primitive roadside campsites, no hookups and several 4x4-only approaches.

name: Pinchot State Forest
why: Formerly Lackawanna State Forest; the Pinchot Trail system and remote ridge-top forest roads above the Wyoming Valley.

name: Caledonia State Park
why: Thaddeus Stevens' iron furnace on the Appalachian Trail, with 35 full-hookup sites across two campgrounds.
rigNote: OUTLIER - 70ft is one or two sites, not the campground. The PA ReserveAmerica feed's longest driveway is 70ft with pull-throughs and a big-rig flag of YES, and 33 of the 165 sites are full-hookup 50-amp. But pulling the agency's own site list for Chinquapin East shows the real spread: 010 is 48ft, 046 is 45ft, 012 is 40ft, and everything else on that page is 13-38ft. Campendium puts the park max at 40ft, with reviewers saying 'most sites are very sloped and short', advising against anything over 25ft, warning that the 150s in Hosack Run are especially bad, and telling people to check driveway lengths when reserving. Route 30 road noise in Chinquapin Hill. Bookable for the coach only in the full-hookup loop, and only with a specific site chosen in advance.

name: Pine Grove Furnace State Park
why: The Appalachian Trail midpoint and AT Museum, two mountain lakes and 70 tent/trailer sites.
rigNote: OUTLIER, and the access is the real problem. Feed max driveway 68ft with pull-throughs across 70 tent/trailer sites; electric on some, no water/sewer, dump station. Campendium's longest reported rig is 42ft and that camper wrote that 'the road through the campground is super tight and despite being very experienced full-time travelers, there were two very close calls.' A 27ft trailer owner reported 'narrow roads and narrow entrances made it tough to get a 27' trailer into a site that was listed as 40'.' A 35ft fifth wheel named 2, 13, 31, 40, 44, 58 and 72 as the sites easiest for big rigs and said the pull-throughs 'looked like they could be difficult for a large rig.' Long sites exist; getting a 40ft coach to them is the risk.

name: Kings Gap Environmental Education Center
why: A stone mansion high on South Mountain with Cumberland Valley overlooks and 25+ miles of trails.

name: Mont Alto State Park
why: Pennsylvania's oldest state park, a 24-acre picnic and trout-fishing spot with a distinctive pavilion.

name: Codorus State Park
why: The 1,275-acre Lake Marburg with 26 miles of shoreline and roughly 180 sites that take rigs up to 50 ft.
rigNote: Genuinely big-rig capable. Feed gives 58ft max RV / 53ft max trailer - the two figures agree, which is the sign of real data rather than a group-site artifact - and the big-rig flag is YES. 192 sites: 31 full-hookup, 78 modern electric (30/50-amp), 58 modern non-electric, 15 tent-only. NO pull-throughs, all back-in. Campendium reviewers confirm 33ft and 35ft rigs fitting easily. ACCESS HAZARD: reviewers warn GPS routes people through Seven Valleys over an 11'1" clearance bridge - a 40ft coach must not follow that routing.

name: Gifford Pinchot State Park
why: A 340-acre lake with 289 macadam-pad campsites, some with sewer/water/electric full hookups.
rigNote: Used the feed's max TRAILER length (60ft) rather than its max RV length (95ft) - the 95 is not a credible driveway and is flagged as an artifact. Big-rig flag YES, 289 sites, 22 with full water/sewer/electric, others 20/30/50-amp; NO pull-throughs. Campendium lists the park max at 45ft, so treat 45-60ft as the honest band. Reviewers: a 32ft Class C with a car dolly and toad found its site 'very spacious and easily accessible', but others report sites with steep grade that 'will not fit a van or small camper' and one having to park at an angle - site selection matters a lot here.

name: Colonel Denning State Park
why: Gateway to the 96,000-acre Tuscarora State Forest, with a 49-site tent-and-trailer campground and the Flat Rock vista hike.
rigNote: Feed max driveway 50ft, but this is a small rustic park and the number should be treated cautiously: 49 sites, NO pull-throughs, no electric/water/sewer hookups at all (water and dump station only), big-rig flag not set. Campendium's longest reported vehicle is a 24ft Class B, whose owner said sites were spacious with little screening and roads were good. No corroborating evidence that anything near 50ft has ever camped here.

name: Cowans Gap State Park
why: A 42-acre lake in Allens Valley ringed by state forest, with 201 sites that take anything from a tent to a large motor home.

name: Little Buffalo State Park
why: Shoaff's Mill and the Blue Ball Tavern alongside a 46-site campground with full-service and electric/water sites.

name: Susquehannock State Park
why: Cliff-top overlooks nearly 400 ft above the Lower Susquehanna River, a prime winter bald-eagle spot.

name: Michaux State Forest
why: 85,000 acres of South Mountain with Pole Steeple, the Appalachian Trail and 27 rustic campsites that accept RVs but have no hookups.
rigNote: Not a campground - DCNR motorized roadside camping. The PA ReserveAmerica listing shows 46 units: 26 State Forest Rustic, 18 Roadside Hike-in, 2 Roadside. The vehicle-accessible sites at the Big Flat, Peggy's Hill and Piney Mountain parking areas are coded 45ft PULL-THROUGH, which is where the 45ft comes from; the hike-in sites carry no length. Gravel forest-road parking areas, no hookups, no water, no facilities of any kind. A 40ft coach would fit the pad but you are dry camping in a state forest parking lot reached by unpaved roads - scout before committing.

name: Tuscarora State Forest
why: Ridge-and-valley forest holding the Hemlocks Natural Area old growth, with primitive roadside sites and no hookups.

name: Babcock State Park
why: Glade Creek Grist Mill, the most-photographed spot in West Virginia, with 52 campsites of which 28 have electric.
rigNote: WV reservation-feed data (mirrored on PerfectCamp) shows 28 of the 52 sites accommodating RVs/trailers between 30 and 50ft; site 30 verified individually at 50ft driveway, back-in, 20/30amp. Official wvstateparks lodging page gives 52 units (28 electric, 24 non-electric) but states no length limit. Season roughly 3rd Friday April through 4th Monday October. ACCESS CAUTION: multiple Campendium reviewers flag the approach off US 60 as effectively one-lane two-way with blind curves for about 5 miles ('a nail biter'); the recommended alternative is WV-41 south then Clifftop Road, which is two real lanes. Campendium's longest reported rig is only 28ft. Reservation length data preferred over the reported figure, but route selection matters more than the number for a 40ft coach.

name: Hawks Nest State Park
why: Aerial tram from a canyon-rim lodge down to the New River, above some of the toughest whitewater in the country.

name: Carnifex Ferry Battlefield State Park
why: An 1861 Civil War battlefield on the rim of the Gauley River Canyon; no overnight accommodations.

name: Little Beaver State Park
why: An 18-acre lake and nearly 20 miles of trail, with 30 electric/water sites, a bathhouse and central dump station.
rigNote: No length limit published by wvstateparks (official page gives 46 sites: 16 water-only, 30 electric+water) and I could not reach per-site driveway lengths in the WV reservation feed, so this is reported tier. Campendium and Roadtrippers both list max RV 45ft, with a verified 45ft longest-rig report (7/13/21) and a camper in a 43ft coach confirming it fit. ACCESS CAUTION: that same 43ft owner wrote 'narrow road with ditches on both sides, had to inch back and forth to get rig in and out' and said the park has 'very few sites that are big rig friendly'; another describes the approach as narrow, curvy, up-then-down. Sites 11-13 and 20 are cited as the more big-rig-workable ones. Many sites need heavy leveling.

name: Bluestone State Park
why: Shoreline park on Bluestone Lake, West Virginia's second-largest body of water, with 82 sites and electric hookups.
rigNote: Applies to Meador Campground, the park's main RV loop. WV reservation-feed data (mirrored on PerfectCamp) shows 21 sites accommodating RVs/trailers between 40 and 60ft; site 20 verified individually at 50ft driveway, back-in, 20/30amp. Official wvstateparks camping page gives Meador 32 sites (7 electric+water, 15 electric-only) with bathhouse and dump station, no stated length limit. CONFLICT: AllStays lists max RV 18ft for Meador - a lower-tier aggregator figure contradicted by both the reservation feed and reviews, and disregarded. IMPORTANT: Old Mill (33 sites) and East Shore (12 sites) campgrounds are CLOSED for Bluestone Dam construction - call 304-466-2805 before relying on this park. Campground roads are paved; one reviewer complained the road in was washed out, others report easy ingress/egress with a large travel trailer.

name: Pipestem Resort State Park
why: Full resort park with an aerial tram down into Bluestone Gorge, two golf courses and an 82-site campground with hookups.

name: Twin Falls Resort State Park
why: Two waterfalls, a pioneer farm and a lodge/golf course, with 50 campsites of which 25 have hookups.

name: Camp Creek State Park and Forest
why: Nearly 6,000 acres with waterfalls, stocked trout streams and 35 miles of trail; 26 electric/water sites plus rustic tent sites.

name: Kanawha State Forest
why: A steep hollow forest 7 miles from downtown Charleston with 46 campsites and 25 RV hookups.
rigNote: DISQUALIFYING. WV State Parks states outright: 'RVs or trailers/truck units longer than 26 feet are not recommended.' 46 sites, 25 with electric and water, two bathhouses, season April-December. ACCESS CAUTION: Campendium reviewers report very narrow roads with tight curves and a steep descent into the forest; one camper with an 18ft trailer nearly got stuck and needed park-office routing, another says 'I would only recommend tents and very small campers (under 20 feet).' Longest rig actually reported is a 20ft Class B. GPS routinely sends drivers through a 9ft x 9ft tunnel that requires an alternate route. Not viable for a 40ft Class A towing a pickup.

name: Greenbrier State Forest
why: Wooded slopes above White Sulphur Springs with cabins and a small 16-unit electric campground.

name: Droop Mountain Battlefield State Park
why: West Virginia's largest Civil War battlefield with a lookout tower and Civil War Discovery Trail interpretation; no overnight stays.

name: Beartown State Park
why: A boardwalk threading a maze of massive sandstone crevices and overhangs on Droop Mountain; no overnight stays.

name: Watoga State Park
why: West Virginia's largest state park, with 88 campsites all on 50-amp electric across the Riverside and Beaver Creek loops.

name: Cacapon Resort State Park
why: Resort park under Cacapon Mountain with a 120-room lodge, cabins, a lake beach and an 18-hole golf course.

name: Berkeley Springs State Park
why: Colonial-era 74-degree mineral springs and a working bathhouse in the middle of town; no overnight accommodations.

name: Douthat State Park
why: A 1936 CCC showpiece with a stocked 50-acre lake and 43+ miles of hiking, biking and bridle trail; most loops cap at 40 ft, Whispering Pines takes 50 ft.
rigNote: DCR states limits per campground: Whispering Pines 50ft max (23 sites, W + 30/50amp, gravel pads) is the ONLY loop rated above 40ft. Lakeside (19 sites), Beaver Dam (14 sites, equestrian, 4 pull-throughs) and White Oak (31 sites, 30amp only) are all capped at 40ft. 87 sites total. ACCESS CAUTION: DCR itself warns White Oak campground is reached over a narrow low-water bridge that can be impassable when flooded - avoid that loop with a 40ft coach. A 40ft Class A fits Whispering Pines, Lakeside or Beaver Dam on the stated limits; book Whispering Pines for margin.

name: Natural Bridge State Park
why: The 200-ft limestone arch over Cedar Creek; the Blue Hollow campsites are primitive and cannot be reached by RV or trailer.

name: James River State Park
why: Three miles of James River frontage, smallmouth fishing and International Dark Sky Park status, with two hookup campgrounds capped at 40 ft.

name: Smith Mountain Lake State Park
why: Virginia's second-largest freshwater lake with a swim beach and 24 hookup RV sites, some taking up to 50 ft.

name: Holliday Lake State Park
why: A quiet 150-acre lake inside Appomattox-Buckingham State Forest; Laurel Ridge takes 40 ft, Redbud 30 ft.

name: Claytor Lake State Park
why: A 4,500-acre New River impoundment built for boating and sport fishing; the Dogwood loop handles RVs up to 40 ft.

name: Fairy Stone State Park
why: Home of the legendary staurolite fairy stones and a 168-acre lake; standard sites cap at 35 ft though equestrian sites take 50 ft.

name: New River Trail State Park
why: A 57-mile rail-trail with tunnels, trestles and the 1807 Shot Tower; the three campsites are primitive with no vehicle access.

name: Grayson Highlands State Park
why: Wild pony herds, 5,000-ft balds beside Mount Rogers and the best bouldering in Virginia; electric/water sites take 40 ft.
rigNote: DCR states up to 40ft at the 38 electric/water sites in Hickory Ridge Campground; no-hookup sites are capped at 30ft (28 sites). Chestnut Hollow is equestrian. Full-service camping May-October only; primitive (no water/hookups) March-April and November. ACCESS CAUTION: the park sits at roughly 3,700-4,900ft and is reached by a sustained steep, curvy mountain climb off US 58 - a Campendium reviewer towing only a 28ft trailer described 'very curvy up and down narrow road' for the final stretch. Campendium's longest reported rig is 38ft and a camp host states only about 10-12 of the 63 sites work reasonably for big rigs; sites are described as skinny and unlevel. A 40ft coach towing a pickup is at the absolute edge here - confirm a specific site. Campground was closed through 1 May 2026 for water/electric/bathhouse rebuild and regrading, so verify it has reopened.

name: Hungry Mother State Park
why: A 108-acre mountain lake with a CCC-built beach and restaurant; most sites cap at 35 ft and Creekside at 30 ft.

name: Sky Meadows State Park
why: Rolling historic farmland in the Blue Ridge foothills and an International Dark Sky Park; camping is hike-in only.

name: Raymond R. "Andy" Guest Jr. Shenandoah River State Park
why: Miles of South Fork Shenandoah frontage with river access, trails and 31 hookup sites taking RVs up to 60 ft.

name: Mount Mitchell State Park
why: The highest peak east of the Mississippi at 6,684 ft, reached by a spur off the Blue Ridge Parkway.

name: Chimney Rock State Park
why: A granite monolith over Hickory Nut Gorge with a 404-ft waterfall and views to Lake Lure; no camping.

name: Gorges State Park
why: Twenty-six waterfalls in a temperate rainforest above Lake Jocassee, with camper cabins and some hookup trailer sites.

name: Lake James State Park
why: A 6,800-acre lake below Linville Gorge with a swim beach and mountain-bike trails; camping is tent and paddle-in.

name: South Mountains State Park
why: The 80-ft High Shoals Falls and nearly 50 miles of hiking, equestrian and bike trail, with some electric trailer sites.

name: Grandfather Mountain State Park
why: Cables-and-ladders ridge scrambling on one of the most rugged and weather-beaten peaks in the Blue Ridge.

name: Elk Knob State Park
why: An amphibolite summit with high-country panoramas, six primitive campsites and good winter snowshoeing.

name: Mount Jefferson State Natural Area
why: A paved summit road to overlooks that reach into Tennessee, over an old-growth oak forest; day use only.

name: New River State Park
why: Paddling on one of the oldest rivers in the world, with drive-in RV/trailer hookup sites and remote paddle-in camps.
rigNote: NC ReserveAmerica feed (via Campflare mirror) gives per-site driveway lengths: site 014-H = 62ft back-in with electric/water/sewer, site 013 = 47ft E/W/S, site 011 = 54ft back-in 50amp. Campflare campground rollup lists 67ft max RV / 55ft trailer; 62ft is the longest I verified at site level. Drive-to RV sites with full hookups are at the US 221 Access Area only - Wagoner Access, Riverbend and Peaks Backcountry are walk-in tent or paddle-in primitive and are not usable by a coach. Dump station and showers on site. No steep or narrow access warnings surfaced; US 221 approach is normal two-lane.

name: Stone Mountain State Park
why: A 600-ft granite dome National Natural Landmark with waterfalls, trout streams and electric/water trailer sites.

name: Harrison Bay State Park
why: A Chickamauga Lake marina park with 128 RV campsites and 27 tent sites twenty minutes from Chattanooga.

name: Booker T. Washington State Park
why: A lakefront day-use park with mountain-bike trails and a boat ramp; overnight is the Oaks group camp only.

name: Savage Gulf State Park
why: The Great Stone Door and 15,000 acres of Cumberland Plateau gorge with 70+ permit-only backcountry sites.

name: Fiery Gizzard State Park
why: The Fiery Gizzard Trail and Foster Falls, one of the highest-rated day hikes in the eastern US.

name: Fall Creek Falls State Park
why: The 256-ft Fall Creek Falls plus a lodge, golf course and 200+ campsites across five camping areas.

name: Hiwassee River State Park
why: State Scenic River float trips out of the Cherokee foothills, with the Gee Creek campground at its base.

name: Fort Loudoun State Historic Park
why: A reconstructed 1756 British frontier fort on the Little Tennessee River in the Overhill Cherokee country.

name: Devil's Den State Park
why: One of the most intact CCC parks in the country, set in Lee Creek Valley among sandstone crevice caves; the approach highways are narrow and steep.

name: Prairie Grove Battlefield State Park
why: One of America's most intact Civil War battlefields, preserving the December 1862 Battle of Prairie Grove.

name: Lake Fort Smith State Park
why: Western terminus of the 240-mile Ozark Highlands Trail, with 30 hookup sites on a mountain reservoir.

name: Hobbs State Park-Conservation Area
why: Arkansas' largest state park at 12,173 acres along Beaver Lake, with hike-in and bike-in camping only.

name: Withrow Springs State Park
why: Floating and smallmouth fishing on War Eagle Creek, with 50-amp full-hookup sites above the bluffs.
rigNote: Arkansas reservation feed (mirrored on Campflare) shows Class AAA full-hookup sites with 50ft driveway / 50ft max RV (sites 21 and 22 both verified individually); 29-30 Class AAA sites with W/S/50amp plus 10 walk-in tent sites. Campflare's campground-level rollup states 65ft, which no individual site I checked supports - treat 50ft as the working number. Official arkansasstateparks/arkansas.com page states no length limit. CONFLICT: The Dyrt claims 'RVs up to 28 feet' and Campendium's longest reported rig is only 35ft (a 35ft fifth wheel, reviewer warned site 19 sits almost perpendicular to the drive and to 'pick a different site if you are longer'). Higher-tier reservation data preferred, but real-world reports cluster well under 50ft, so a 40ft coach plus towed pickup should confirm a specific site by phone (479-559-2593). Approach is via AR-23 and some gravel county roads; no steep-grade warnings found.

name: Petit Jean State Park
why: Arkansas' first state park, with 95-ft Cedar Falls, historic Mather Lodge and 55 full-hookup sites on the mountain top.

name: Mount Nebo State Park
why: A bench-trail loop and hang-gliding launches on a flat-topped mountain reached by the hairpin switchbacks of Highway 155.

name: Lake Dardanelle State Park
why: A 34,300-acre Arkansas River reservoir known for bass tournaments, with 50-amp full-hookup sites.

name: Pinnacle Mountain State Park
why: A cone-shaped peak over the Arkansas River with the Arkansas Arboretum and steep summit trails; day use only.

name: Woolly Hollow State Park
why: The 40-acre Lake Bennett with a swim beach, an 1882 log cabin and 50-amp full-hookup sites.

name: Mount Magazine State Park
why: Arkansas' highest point at 2,753 ft, with a cliff-edge lodge, technical rock climbing and hang gliding.

name: Bull Shoals-White River State Park
why: World-class White River trout fishing at the foot of Bull Shoals Dam, with 63 full-hookup sites.

name: Lake Ouachita State Park
why: Forty thousand acres of exceptionally clear water ringed by the Ouachita National Forest, with 50-amp sewer sites.

name: Lake Catherine State Park
why: A 1930s CCC park holding the lake's only full-service marina, with 50-amp sewer sites and cabins.

name: DeGray Lake Resort State Park
why: An island lodge and world-class mountain-bike trail network on a 13,800-acre lake, with 50-amp sewer sites.

name: Crater of Diamonds State Park
why: The only place in the world where the public can dig for real diamonds and keep what they find.

name: Daisy State Park
why: Lake Greeson crappie and bass fishing with an adjacent ATV/4x4 trail system in the Ouachitas.

name: Queen Wilhelmina State Park
why: A lodge atop Rich Mountain, Arkansas' second-highest peak, midway along the Talimena Scenic Drive.

name: Cossatot River State Park-Natural Area
why: Cossatot Falls, a rocky canyon of Class IV-V rapids, with tent-only camping at Sandbar, the Falls and Ed Banks.

name: Tok River State Recreation Site
why: First Alaska state campground inside the border at Alaska Highway mile 1309, with 27 sites and six pull-throughs built for motor homes up to 60 feet.

name: Eagle Trail State Recreation Site
why: Wooded 35-site campground on the Tok Cutoff that BC Parks' Alaska counterpart bills as the first chance to walk into the Alaska Range.

name: Moon Lake State Recreation Site
why: Fifteen-site campground on a warm float-plane lake with a sandy beach, the local swimming hole west of Tok.
rigNote: Official DNR page states 'No RV size limit'. Campendium 'longest vehicle reported' = 22 ft (2018 travel trailer, 'Sites are nicely spaced apart. Easy to navigate and set up') and flags 'Big rigs' as an amenity. 22 ft is the largest logged stay, not a posted maximum - a 40 ft coach is unverified here.

name: Porcupine Creek State Recreation Site
why: Twelve-site creekside campground on the Nabesna Road side of the Tok Cutoff, used as a staging point for Wrangell-St. Elias.

name: Chena River State Recreation Site
why: Day-use river park inside Fairbanks with a boat launch, 30 picnic sites and walking trails along the Chena.

name: Chena Pump Wayside State Recreation Site
why: Small Fairbanks day-use wayside with a beach boat launch and picnic shelters on the lower Chena River.

name: Salcha River State Recreation Site
why: Six-site campground and busy boat launch known for an excellent grayling fishery and a July king salmon run.
rigNote: Official DNR page states 'No RV size limit'. Campendium longest vehicle reported = 38 ft (2023 fifth-wheel) with 'plenty of flat spots for rigs of all sizes' on the gravel bar; another notes 'boat parking sites (good for big rigs)'; a 35 ft fifth-wheel used the riverside overflow. Big-rig capacity is largely in the gravel bar / overflow areas rather than numbered sites.

name: Lower Chatanika River State Recreation Area
why: Olnes Pond and Whitefish campgrounds north of Fairbanks on the Elliott Highway, popular for fishing and gold-country day trips.
rigNote: Official DNR pages for both campgrounds - Olnes Pond (15 sites) and Whitefish (25 sites) - state 'No RV size limit' but publish no number. First-come, first-served, no online reservations, so no per-site reservation data exists. Good Sam listing has no length field. Nothing credible found.

name: Harding Lake State Recreation Area
why: Big clear lake off the Richardson Highway with 90-plus campsites, a boat launch and nature trails.
rigNote: Conservative figure. The only unit in the ReserveAmerica system - site 156, Group Camping Area - is listed at 35 ft, pull-through. The 78 first-come vehicle sites are not in the reservation system and the official DNR page posts 'No RV size limit' plus 'Many vehicle sites are large enough to accommodate large motor homes or trailers', so the true site maximum may be higher than 35 ft but is unpublished. Sources conflict; higher tier (official) is qualitative only.

name: Upper Chatanika River State Recreation Site
why: Twenty-four-site campground on the Steese Highway that is the classic put-in for Chatanika River floats.
rigNote: Official DNR page states 'No RV size limit' with no number. Alaska.org: '24 wooded sites along the Upper Chatanika River', 'suitable for tents and RVs'. No Campendium listing with length data, no reservation system (first-come). Nothing credible found.

name: Chena River State Recreation Area
why: 254,000-acre recreation area up Chena Hot Springs Road with Rosehip, Granite Tors and Red Squirrel campgrounds, grayling water and the Granite Tors trail.

name: Birch Lake State Recreation Site
why: Twenty-four-site lakeside campground on the Richardson Highway popular with anglers, jet skiers and water skiers.

name: Matanuska Glacier State Recreation Site
why: Six-site campground and overlook on the Glenn Highway Scenic Byway with an interpretive trail facing the Matanuska Glacier.

name: King Mountain State Recreation Site
why: Twenty-two-site campground on the Matanuska River at Chickaloon; Alaska State Parks states there is no RV size limit here.

name: Independence Mine State Historical Park
why: Preserved 1930s hard-rock gold camp high in Hatcher Pass, with guided tours and alpine trails but no camping.

name: Summit Lake State Recreation Site
why: Day-use alpine site at the top of Hatcher Pass, known for wildflower tundra and paragliding launches.

name: Hatcher Pass East Management Area
why: Alpine management area with 30-plus summits, gold-rush relics and the small Government Peak Campground on the Little Susitna.

name: Rocky Lake State Recreation Site
why: Quiet 10-site lake campground near Big Lake with a 30-foot vehicle limit and no jet boats or jet skis allowed.

name: Big Lake North State Recreation Site
why: Sixty-site campground on Big Lake, the Mat-Su's year-round boating and watersports playground.
rigNote: Official DNR page states 'No RV size limit' but no number. Alaska.org describes '60 wooded sites... suitable for tents and RVs'. Campendium listing exists but the 'Longest Vehicle Reported' field is empty and there are no big-rig comments. Nothing credible found.

name: Nancy Lake State Recreation Area
why: Drumlin-and-lake country west of Willow with the 98-site South Rolly campground and a famous canoe-trail system.
rigNote: Applies to South Rolly Lake Campground, the SRA's main road-accessible campground; official DNR pages for both the SRA and South Rolly state 'No RV size limit'. Campendium: a 32 ft fifth-wheel reported 'Pull through sites are considered premium... they were really the only semi-easy option for our 32ft fifth wheel', and another reviewer calls it 'a better fit for big rigs than the Nancy Lake campground'. Warning: 'gravel road throughout is severely potholed'.

name: Nancy Lake State Recreation Site
why: Thirty-site roadside campground on the Parks Highway at Nancy Lake, separate from the larger recreation area.
rigNote: Big-rig-hostile. Official DNR page states 'No RV size limit', but Campendium longest vehicle reported = 27 ft and reviews are explicit: a 32 ft fifth-wheel 'ended up only doing a drive through as spots were too small... most spots were too narrow for our slides'; another says 'The loops and sites are quite small... If you are towing anything larger than 30 ft, you best be experienced at it.' Do not take a 40 ft coach in.

name: Matanuska Lakes State Recreation Area
why: Stocked trout lakes between Palmer and Wasilla with 17 sites and an easy hiking and biking trail network.
rigNote: Official DNR page lists '9 RV Sites' and '8 Campsites' with a 7-day limit but carries no RV size limit field at all (unlike sister Mat-Su units). No Campendium length data, no reservation per-site data. Nothing credible found.

name: Finger Lake State Recreation Site
why: Twenty-four-site lake campground near Palmer; the RV loop is capped at 35 feet and the tent loop at 20.

name: Chugach State Park
why: Half-million-acre mountain park on Anchorage's doorstep with Bird Creek, Eagle River and Eklutna Lake campgrounds and hundreds of trail miles.
rigNote: Park-wide figure is the highest posted campground limit. Alaska DNR posts: Eklutna Lake Campground 'RV Length Limit - 30ft'; Bird Creek Campground "35' RV size limit"; Eagle River Campground 'No RV size limit' (no number given, so unverified for 40 ft). Reservation system only lists cabins and the group area (20 ft pull-through). A 40 ft coach is explicitly excluded from Eklutna Lake and Bird Creek; Eagle River is the only possible option and is unconfirmed.

name: Willow Creek State Recreation Area
why: Sprawling 140-site camping area at the Susitna confluence, one of the busiest salmon-fishing spots on the Parks Highway.

name: Montana Creek State Recreation Site
why: Thirty-six-site campground at a well-known Parks Highway salmon creek south of Talkeetna.
rigNote: Official DNR page states 'No RV size limit', but gives no number. Campendium has no length logged and reviews are discouraging for a 40-footer: 'The spaces are small and pretty crowded', 'set up like a parking lot with hardly any space', 'If you have a large RV it will be snug but smart parking and site selection works.' Big-rig-marginal.

name: Denali State Park
why: 325,000-acre park straddling the Parks Highway with Byers Lake, K'esugi Ken, Lower Troublesome Creek and the Denali View campgrounds and the Kesugi Ridge traverse.

name: Liberty Falls State Recreation Site
why: Ten-site campground in a tight canyon beside Liberty Falls on the Edgerton Highway to Chitina.

name: Squirrel Creek State Recreation Site
why: Twenty-five-site Richardson Highway campground bounded by Squirrel Creek and the Tonsina River, stocked for grayling.
rigNote: Official DNR page states 'No RV size limit'. Campendium longest vehicle reported = 38 ft (2023 fifth-wheel, fit successfully); listing flags 'Big rigs'. Counterpoint from a 23 ft Class B+ camper: 'Sites are generally on smaller side and not very level.' Site selection matters for a 40 ft coach.

name: Worthington Glacier State Recreation Site
why: Roadside day-use site in Thompson Pass where you can walk almost to the toe of Worthington Glacier.

name: Blueberry Lake State Recreation Site
why: High alpine 25-site campground in Thompson Pass above Valdez, known for grayling and enormous snowfall.

name: Ninilchik State Recreation Area
why: Cluster of beach, river and bluff campgrounds around the old Russian village of Ninilchik, the hub of Cook Inlet halibut charters.

name: Deep Creek State Recreation Area
why: Hundred-site beach camping area legendary for halibut and king salmon and for its tractor-launched dory fleet; 35-foot RV limit.

name: Stariski State Recreation Site
why: Thirteen sites on a high bluff over Cook Inlet with volcano views; 35-foot RV limit.

name: Clam Gulch State Recreation Area
why: Bluff-top campground above the beach that made Alaska's razor-clam reputation; 120 sites, 35-foot RV limit.

name: Johnson Lake State Recreation Area
why: Fifty-one wooded sites on a stocked rainbow-trout lake near Kasilof; 35-foot RV limit.

name: Kasilof River State Recreation Site
why: Day-use river access with 25 sites, heavily used by Kasilof River fishing guides and drift boaters.

name: Crooked Creek State Recreation Site
why: Seventy-nine sites at the Kasilof-Crooked Creek confluence, busiest in May and June for kings; 35-foot RV limit.

name: Old Kasilof Landing State Recreation Site
why: Twelve-site day-use drift-boat retrieval landing on the lower Kasilof River.

name: Captain Cook State Recreation Area
why: Quiet forest-and-beach park at the end of the Kenai Spur Highway with Discovery Campground and Cook Inlet views.

name: Kenai River Special Management Area
why: State-managed corridor along the Kenai River with the Bing's Landing, Morgan's Landing, Izaak Walton and Funny River campgrounds.
rigNote: Alaska DNR page for Bing's Landing (36 campsites) posts no RV size limit. Campendium longest vehicle reported = 40 ft; a 40 ft fifth-wheel reviewer wrote 'Campground is a loop with large, nicely spaced sites... Almost any size rig could fit here'; a 35 ft rig also reported good interior roads. Applies to Bing's Landing specifically - Morgan's Landing, Izaak Walton and Funny River campgrounds in the same SMA have no length data.

name: Anchor River State Recreation Area
why: Forty-six sites strung along the beach at the most westerly point on the North American highway system, king-salmon and volcano-view country.
rigNote: Sources conflict. Official DNR marks the SRA and the Coho, Silver King and Steelhead campgrounds 'RV size limit - campers'; Halibut and Slidehole campgrounds are marked 'No RV size limit'. A 2023 Campendium reviewer states 'This campground [Halibut] is no longer big rig friendly - meaning over 35 Ft. Only a couple of sites can be used'; another notes 'Some of the sites are pretty short'. Longest rig actually logged on Campendium is only 24 ft. Treat 35 ft as the practical ceiling; a 40 ft coach would be limited to a couple of sites at best.

name: Eveline State Recreation Site
why: Day-use meadow above Kachemak Bay known for wildflowers and easy winter cross-country skiing.

name: Kachemak Bay State Park
why: Alaska's first state park, roughly 400,000 boat- or air-access acres of glaciers and fjords across the bay from Homer.

name: Kachemak Bay State Wilderness Park
why: Wilderness half of the Kachemak Bay complex, reached only by water taxi or floatplane from Homer.

name: Lowell Point State Recreation Site
why: Day-use beach south of Seward and the trailhead for the tidal coastal route to Caines Head.

name: Caines Head State Recreation Area
why: Abandoned WWII Fort McGilvray above Resurrection Bay, reached by a tide-dependent beach hike or boat from Seward.

name: Watson Lake Campground
why: Forty-site territorial campground on the south shore of Watson Lake with eight pull-throughs, the standard first night in Yukon.

name: Liard Canyon Recreation Site
why: Day-use site at Lucky Lake with a 2.2 km forest trail to a viewpoint over the Liard River canyon.

name: Big Creek Campground
why: Fifteen sites, seven of them pull-through, right at the edge of a shallow rocky creek on the Alaska Highway.
rigNote: No length data. Official yukon.ca: 'Total sites: 15', 'Pull through: 7', no posted length limit; 'some campsites right at the water's edge'. First-come only so no reservation data; no Campendium listing found (constructed URL 404); campgroundsalaska and allstays pages are robots-blocked. 7 of 15 sites being pull-through is a favourable sign but is not a length figure.

name: Simpson Lake Campground
why: Ten-site campground on the Campbell Highway north of Watson Lake, a favourite angling and hunting base with nesting loons.

name: Wolf Creek Campground
why: Forty-six sites with 11 pull-throughs just south of Whitehorse, one of six reservable Yukon campgrounds.

name: Kookatsoon Lake Recreation Site
why: Small sandy day-use beach on a warm shallow lake, the family swimming spot south of Whitehorse.

name: Marsh Lake Campground
why: Sixty-six lakeside sites with nine pull-throughs, reservable, and a spring swan-viewing draw.
rigNote: Official yukon.ca lists 66 total sites and 9 pull-throughs, no posted length limit. Campendium longest vehicle reported = 43 ft; reviewers describe 'roomy' sites, 'back-in site but there are also pull through as well for big motor homes', a 32 ft Class C with tow vehicle at site 28 ('nice and level and spacious'), and a 35 ft RV. Best big-rig prospect of the five Yukon campgrounds in this list.

name: Marsh Lake Recreation Site
why: Popular summer beach on Marsh Lake with tent camping and swan migration viewing.

name: Lake Laberge Campground
why: Sixteen sites on the lake immortalised in Robert Service's Cremation of Sam McGee.
rigNote: No length data. Official yukon.ca: 'Total sites: 16', 'Pull through: 1', no reservable sites, no posted length limit. First-come only so no reservation per-site data exists; allstays and campgroundsalaska pages are robots-blocked; no Campendium listing found. A 16-site campground with a single pull-through is high-risk for a 40 ft coach plus toad.

name: Takhini River Campground
why: Twelve back-in sites in Kusawa Territorial Park, the usual put-in and take-out for Takhini River paddlers.

name: Kusawa Lake Campground
why: Fifty-three sites on a long glacial lake with Dall sheep on the slopes; Yukon states a 32 ft (9.7 m) maximum RV length.

name: Tagish Bridge Recreation Site
why: Day-use site at the Tagish narrows, a well-known lake trout, whitefish and grayling spot.

name: Fox Lake Campground
why: Forty-three sites with nine pull-throughs right off the Klondike Highway on a boating lake.

name: Conrad Campground
why: Yukon's newest campground, 35 sites on Windy Arm below the old Conrad silver workings near Carcross.

name: Pine Lake Campground
why: Forty-two sites and a day-use beach minutes from Haines Junction with a full view of the Kluane and St. Elias ranges.

name: Spruce Beetle Trail Recreation Site
why: Two-kilometre interpretive loop on the Alaska Highway explaining the spruce beetle outbreak that reshaped this forest.

name: Otter Falls Recreation Site
why: The waterfall that appeared on the 1954 Canadian five-dollar bill, up the gravel Aishihik Road.

name: Dezadeash Lake Campground
why: Twenty back-in sites on one of Yukon's warmer, shallower lakes on the Haines Road, good lake trout water.
rigNote: Official yukon.ca: 'Total sites: 20', 'Pull through: 0', no posted length limit; warns the area 'is known for high winds'. Campendium longest vehicle reported = 27 ft (truck camper, 'Level site... Easy to access off the Highway'); next largest logged is 25 ft. Zero pull-throughs plus no documented rig over 27 ft makes this a poor bet for a 40 ft coach.

name: Congdon Creek Campground
why: 103 sites on Kluane Lake with 26 pull-throughs; tenting is confined to an electric-fenced compound because of heavy grizzly use.

name: Million Dollar Falls Campground
why: Thirty-four back-in sites on the Haines Road with a boardwalk to a lookout over a 60 m waterfall on the Takhanne River.

name: Yukon River Campground
why: Yukon's largest campground, 102 sites with 20 pull-throughs across the ferry from Dawson City beside the sternwheeler graveyard.

name: Klondike River Campground
why: Thirty-five sites east of Dawson with a 1.7 km boardwalk through old-growth forest the dredges never touched.
rigNote: Yukon government campgrounds are first-come with no reservation system, so no per-site pad data exists. Official yukon.ca page gives 'Total sites: 35' and 'Pull through: 2' and no length restriction. No Campendium listing found (constructed URLs 404). Nothing credible found - but note only 2 pull-throughs for a 40 ft coach plus toad.

name: Tombstone Mountain Campground
why: Fifty-one sites at Dempster Highway km 71, the base for Tombstone Territorial Park hiking and Dempster trips.

name: Bow Valley Provincial Park
why: Montane grassland park at the Bow and Kananaskis confluence with three reservable campgrounds and four group areas.

name: Bow Valley Wildland Provincial Park
why: Wildland park wrapping the Bow Valley peaks, backcountry camping only, home to the Ha Ling and Wind Valley trails.

name: Canmore Nordic Centre Provincial Park
why: 1988 Olympic cross-country venue above Canmore, now a day-use hub for world-class mountain biking and ski trails.

name: Spray Valley Provincial Park
why: Long park along the Smith-Dorrien road and Spray Lakes Reservoir, the quiet back way between Canmore and Kananaskis Lakes.

name: Peter Lougheed Provincial Park
why: Alberta's largest provincial park, the Kananaskis Lakes core with several big campgrounds and an alpine trail network.

name: Ghost River Wilderness Area
why: Strictly protected wilderness area northeast of Banff; foot access and random backcountry camping only.

name: Bragg Creek Provincial Park
why: Elbow River day-use park at Bragg Creek, the eastern gateway into Kananaskis Country.

name: William A. Switzer Provincial Park
why: Chain of five lakes north of Hinton with several campgrounds and the Athabasca Lookout, a common Jasper overflow base.

name: Rock Lake Provincial Park
why: Drive-in campsites on a turquoise lake at the edge of Willmore Wilderness, a staging area for trails and a popular fishing lake.

name: Police Outpost Provincial Park
why: Prairie-and-lake park hard on the Montana border with a campground, big Chief Mountain views and heavy birdlife.
rigNote: No posted length limit found. Alberta Parks own park page is robots-blocked; Travel Alberta lists 46 unserviced sites 'suitable for both tents and RVs'. Campendium 'longest vehicle reported' = 25 ft (travel trailer, 2022) - that is the biggest rig campers have logged, NOT a stated maximum. No credible evidence either way for a 40 ft coach.

name: Beauvais Lake Provincial Park
why: Aspen-parkland lake park southwest of Pincher Creek known for birds and wildlife and year-round recreation.

name: Woolford Provincial Park
why: Small cottonwood-shaded campground on the St. Mary River east of Cardston.
rigNote: No posted length limit found (Alberta Parks page robots-blocked). Campendium 'longest vehicle reported' = 23 ft (2019, site 12); reviewer notes access is 'about 5 miles off paved road in gravel'. Small day-use-scale campground; treat as unproven for a 40 ft coach.

name: Castle Provincial Park
why: Big 2017 park in the Castle drainage with the 96-site Beaver Mines Lake and Castle Falls campgrounds and designated random camping areas.
rigNote: No length data found from any tier. Alberta Parks pages are robots-blocked and shop.albertaparks.ca / reserveamerica mirror both refused fetch (403 / cert mismatch). Travel Alberta says Beaver Mines Lake campground has '76 unserviced sites suitable for RVs and tents'; Alberta Campground Guide lists 96 sites. Castle Falls and Castle River Bridge campgrounds also exist. No maximum unit length published anywhere I could reach.

name: Castle Wildland Provincial Park
why: Wildland half of the Castle, protecting watersheds and habitat for more than 200 rare species including grizzly and wolverine.

name: Moonshine Lake Provincial Park
why: Boreal lake park in the Peace Country west of Grande Prairie, stocked for trout.

name: Muncho Lake Park
why: Jade-green 12 km lake at Alaska Highway km 681 with the Strawberry Flats and MacDonald campgrounds and the best Stone sheep and caribou viewing on the road.

name: Toad River Hot Springs Park
why: Undeveloped hot-springs park off the Alaska Highway near Toad River with no vehicle-accessible campground in BC Parks' operations data.

name: Stone Mountain Park
why: Summit Lake campground at the highest point on the Alaska Highway, 28 sites in alpine terrain with the Flower Springs Lake trail.

name: Liard River Hot Springs Park
why: The 53-site campground at the Alaska Highway's most famous stop, a boardwalk through a warm-water swamp to the Alpha and Beta hot pools.

name: Liard River Corridor Park
why: Large river-corridor wilderness park east of the hot springs with no vehicle-accessible campground listed by BC Parks.

name: Liard River West Corridor Park
why: Undeveloped western extension of the Liard River corridor protection, no listed campground or day-use facilities.

name: Smith River Falls - Fort Halkett Park
why: Two-tier Smith River waterfall and the site of the 1829 HBC Fort Halkett, reached by a rough side road off the Alaska Highway.

name: Swan Lake Park
why: Forty-four-site reservable campground on a warm Peace Country lake south of Dawson Creek, good swimming and birding.
rigNote: BC Parks page gives no length (only a 2018 campground map PDF). Campendium longest vehicle reported = 31 ft: 'We are 31ft and we had plenty of room however some of the twin sites were on the smaller side.' Listing flags 'Big rigs'. 40 ft unverified.

name: Kiskatinaw Park
why: Twenty-eight sites beside the curved wooden Kiskatinaw Bridge on the original 1942 Alaska Highway alignment.
rigNote: Big-rig-hostile per campers. BC Parks page gives no length; reservation API refused fetch (403). Campendium 'Longest Vehicle Reported' is blank and a reviewer states 'Most of the sites are too small for a bigger RV.' Access is via the Old Alaska Highway loop. No number found.

name: Kiskatinaw River Park
why: River-canyon conservation park north of Dawson Creek with no vehicle-accessible campground listed by BC Parks.

name: Peace River Corridor Park
why: Riverbank park protecting Peace River bottomland habitat; no campground listed in BC Parks' operations data.

name: Beatton River Park
why: Undeveloped Beatton River park in the Peace lowlands, no listed campground or day-use facilities.

name: One Island Lake Park
why: Twenty-eight-site first-come campground on a quiet trout lake southeast of Dawson Creek.
rigNote: No length data. BC Parks page has no camping specs; reservation API refused fetch (403). Campendium lists 30 sites with the 'Longest Vehicle Reported' field empty and no big-rig comments. Nothing credible found.

name: East Pine Park
why: Boat-launch park at the Murray and Pine river confluence; no campground listed by BC Parks.

name: Pine River Breaks Park
why: Steep eroded Pine River breaks protected for wildlife habitat, with no developed facilities listed.

name: Gwillim Lake Park
why: Fifty reservable sites on a deep lake in the Rocky Mountain foothills south of Chetwynd, known for burbot and lake trout.

name: Beatton Park
why: Thirty-nine sites on Charlie Lake with a swimming beach and a big winter cross-country ski trail network.

name: Charlie Lake Park
why: Fifty-seven-site reservable campground on the lake just north of Fort St. John, with a steep trail to the shore.

name: Ta Ch'ila Park (Boya Lake Park)
why: Forty-four sites on the Cassiar Highway's famous aquamarine lake, prized for water clarity, canoeing and warm swimming.
rigNote: Number is soft - read the caveats. Campendium longest vehicle reported = 50 ft; a 55 ft Class A parked in a lakeside lot with 'simple' backup access, a 34 ft Class A used a pull-through, a 33 ft Class A got in but called the roads 'narrow'. Against that: 'I wouldn't recommend bigger rvs to go here. Small sites and steep grade in' (from a 50 ft toy-hauler owner) and 'Most of the back-ins are not suited to bigger rigs (even if not towing)'. A 40 ft coach should target a pull-through and expect a steep, narrow entry road.

name: Hyland River Park
why: Small Alaska Highway riverside park near the Yukon border with no campground listed in BC Parks' operations data.

name: Tuya Mountains Park
why: Remote subglacial volcano landscape west of the Cassiar Highway; no road access and no developed facilities.

name: Stikine River Park
why: Protects the Grand Canyon of the Stikine, a 90 km unrunnable gorge; wilderness access only, no campground listed.

name: Bear Glacier Park
why: Roadside viewpoint park on Highway 37A where Bear Glacier calves into Strohn Lake, no campground listed.

name: Meziadin Lake Park
why: Sixty-six reservable sites at the Highway 37 junction, the standard base for the run into Stewart and Hyder.
rigNote: BC Parks page gives no length; Camping & RVing BC confirms 66 sites with 30 amp power. Campendium longest vehicle reported = 40 ft - a 40 ft fifth-wheel backed into site 15 and found it 'easy to access and level'. Gravel, level sites. Caveats: a 32 ft rig called the sites 'just big enough' and warned of a 'tight fit' for bigger rigs in the lakeside circle (sites 50-58), and 'many of the spots are better off for smaller rigs'.

name: Border Lake Park
why: Small remote park on the Alaska border north of Stewart with no developed facilities listed.

name: Lava Forks Park
why: Protects Canada's most recent volcanic eruption site on the Iskut-Unuk divide; no road access or facilities listed.

name: Tyhee Lake Park
why: Seventy-one-site reservable campground at Telkwa with a swimming beach and boat launch, the go-to family park near Smithers.

name: Call Lake Park
why: Small lake park just outside Smithers with no vehicle-accessible campground listed by BC Parks.

name: Red Bluff Park
why: Thirty-four sites on Babine Lake at Granisle, under a red volcanic bluff, known for lake trout and rainbow fishing.

name: Old Man Lake Park
why: Remote small lake park south of Houston with no developed campground listed by BC Parks.

name: Seven Sisters Park
why: The seven-summit massif above the Skeena between Smithers and Terrace; hiking and climbing, no developed campground listed.

name: Seeley Lake Park
why: Twenty first-come sites on a small lake in the Seeley Lake valley near Hazelton with a good interpretive trail.
rigNote: Campendium 'longest vehicle reported' field = 26 ft, but review text documents a larger successful stay: a 32 ft Class C with a towed vehicle attached found 'several fairly level sites'. Same reviewer: 'all sites are back in (contrary to one review there is no pull through site) and many of them are somewhat steep.' Another reviewer recommends the park 'to anyone with an RV 35' or less'. Treat 35 ft as an informal ceiling; a 40 ft coach plus toad is likely too long.

name: Anderson Flats Park
why: Bulkley River flats park near New Hazelton protecting wetland habitat; no campground listed.

name: Bulkley Junction Park
why: Small park at the Bulkley and Skeena junction with no developed facilities listed by BC Parks.

name: Ross Lake Park
why: Small day-use lake park near New Hazelton with no campground listed in BC Parks' operations data.

name: Boulder Creek Park
why: Roadside creek park on Highway 16 east of Hazelton, no developed campground listed.

name: Netalzul Meadows Park
why: Wet meadow complex on the Bulkley protected for waterfowl; no developed facilities listed.

name: Nilkitkwa Lake Park
why: Remote lake park at the north end of Babine Lake reached by forest road; no campground listed.

name: Rainbow Alley Park
why: Short river between Babine and Nilkitkwa lakes famous for rainbow trout; no developed campground listed.

name: Kitwanga Mountain Park
why: Grassy south-facing mountain above the Skeena at Kitwanga; no developed facilities listed.

name: Nadina Mountain Park
why: Isolated mountain park south of Houston with no road access or developed facilities listed.

name: West Lake Park
why: Popular Prince George swimming and day-use lake southwest of town; no vehicle campground listed by BC Parks.

name: Fort George Canyon Park
why: Fraser River canyon that wrecked sternwheelers, reached by a 4 km trail south of Prince George.

name: Eskers Park
why: Glacial esker ridges and lakes north of Prince George, a big local hiking, biking and ski trail network.

name: Dahl Lake Park
why: Remote wetland and lake park west of Prince George with no developed facilities listed.

name: Three Sisters Lakes Park
why: Three small kettle lakes south of Prince George with no developed campground listed.

name: Fraser River Park
why: Undeveloped Fraser River bank park south of Prince George; no facilities listed by BC Parks.

name: Bobtail Mountain Park
why: Forested mountain park in the Nechako plateau with no road access or developed facilities listed.

name: Purden Lake Park
why: Seventy-eight reservable sites on a warm lake on Highway 16 east of Prince George, the main highway camp toward McBride.
rigNote: Strongest BC evidence in this batch. Campendium longest vehicle reported = 40 ft, and the reviewer was a 40 ft Class A towing a car - exactly this rig configuration - who stayed successfully (they were charged an extra ~$11 CAD for the Class A plus toad). A 34 ft Class A also reported a good stay; listing flags 'Big rigs'. BC Parks page itself publishes no length.

name: Stuart River Park
why: Canoe-route park along the fur-brigade Stuart River; no vehicle-accessible campground listed.

name: Crooked River Park
why: Sixty-five reservable sites at Bear Lake on Highway 97, the standard first stop heading north from Prince George.

name: Sugarbowl-Grizzly Den Park
why: Alpine hiking and backcountry ski park in the Cariboo Mountains with huts but no vehicle campground.

name: Wells Gray Park
why: BC's waterfall park, 167 campsites across Pyramid, Clearwater Lake and Falls Creek, with Helmcken Falls and Murtle Lake canoeing.

name: North Thompson River Park
why: Sixty-one-site reservable campground at Clearwater where the Clearwater meets the North Thompson.
rigNote: BC Parks page gives no length. Campendium longest vehicle reported = 34 ft (2023 Class A, site 42, 'large sites', 'very private') and a camper notes the drives are 'all asphalt... easy to get around with a big rig'. Caveats: 'riverfront sites are generally smaller (except for site 27)' with rigs over 22 ft advised away from them, and the park has 'some really small sites' - site selection is critical.

name: Dunn Peak Park
why: Alpine ridge park east of Little Fort with no road access or developed facilities listed.

name: Caligata Lake Park
why: Remote small lake park east of Clearwater with no developed campground listed.

name: Taweel Park
why: Backcountry lake-chain canoe park on the Bonaparte Plateau; no vehicle campground listed.

name: Eakin Creek Canyon Park
why: Short canyon and waterfall park off Highway 24 with no developed campground listed.

name: Eakin Creek Floodplain Park
why: Old-growth cedar floodplain on Eakin Creek, a small conservation park with no facilities listed.

name: Emar Lakes Park
why: Small lakes and wetlands on the Bonaparte Plateau reached on foot; no developed facilities listed.

name: North Thompson Islands Park
why: River islands protected for wildlife south of Clearwater; no developed facilities listed.

name: Chu Chua Cottonwood Park
why: Rare black cottonwood floodplain forest on the North Thompson with no developed campground listed.

name: High Lakes Basin Park
why: Plateau lake basin off Highway 24 with rustic access and no developed campground listed.

name: Donnely Lake Park
why: Small plateau lake park northwest of Clearwater with no developed facilities listed.

name: Wire Cache Park
why: Remote park in the Adams River headwaters with no road access or facilities listed.

name: Bridge Lake Park
why: Sixteen first-come sites on Bridge Lake on Highway 24, the Fishing Highway, with a boat launch.
rigNote: No length data. BC Parks page has no camping specs; reservation API refused fetch (403). Campendium lists 13 campsites with the 'Longest Vehicle Reported' field blank and no large-RV comments at all. Nothing credible found.

name: Rainbow/Q'iwentem Park
why: Quesnel Lake area conservation park with no developed campground listed by BC Parks.

name: Quesnel Lake Park
why: Protects shoreline on North America's deepest fjord lake; no vehicle-accessible campground listed.

name: Finn Creek Park
why: Small North Thompson tributary park north of Clearwater with no developed campground listed.

name: Upper Adams River Park
why: Protects upper Adams River salmon spawning habitat; no developed campground listed.

name: Canim Beach Park
why: Sandy beach day-use park on Canim Lake in the South Cariboo; no vehicle campground listed.

name: Bonaparte Park
why: Large rolling plateau park of small lakes and meadows reached by forest road; no developed campground listed.

name: Ruth Lake Park
why: Small Cariboo lake park near Forest Grove with no developed campground listed.

name: Schoolhouse Lake Park
why: Remote Cariboo plateau lake park with no road-accessible campground listed.

name: Green Lake Park
why: 124 reservable sites in three campgrounds around a big turquoise Cariboo lake near 70 Mile House.

name: Blue River Pine Park
why: Rare interior ponderosa-type pine stand at Blue River; small conservation park with no campground listed.

name: Blue River Black Spruce Park
why: Black spruce bog beside Highway 5 at Blue River, protected as an ecosystem sample; no campground listed.

name: Tsintsunko Lakes Park
why: Bonaparte Plateau lakes park reached by forest road with no developed campground listed.

name: Momich Lakes Park
why: Twenty rustic sites on Momich and Cayenne lakes reached by a long forest road east of Barriere.

name: Pukeashun Park
why: Mountain park between the Adams and Seymour valleys with no road access or facilities listed.

name: Mud Lake Delta Park
why: Wetland delta on the North Thompson at Blue River, protected for waterfowl; no facilities listed.

name: Oregana Creek Park
why: Small headwaters park in the Monashees with no road access or facilities listed.

name: Upper Seymour River Park
why: Old-growth cedar-hemlock valley at the head of Seymour Arm; no developed campground listed.

name: Crater Lake Park
why: Small Cariboo lake park near Bridge Lake with no developed campground listed.

name: Mount Robson Park
why: The 3,954 m highest peak in the Canadian Rockies, 203 campsites and the Berg Lake Trail, right on Highway 16 at the Jasper boundary.
rigNote: Two frontcountry campgrounds; BC Parks page publishes no lengths and the reservation API refused fetch (403). Robson Meadows: Campendium max reported 28 ft but reviewers report 'All sites are back in and were long, level and big rig friendly' and a 33 ft RV stayed two nights. Robson River: Campendium max reported 32 ft, 'Long level sites', two pull-throughs, sites 20-41 have 30/50 amp; heavy Hwy 16 traffic noise. 33 ft is the largest rig actually documented, not a posted cap.

name: Mount Robson Corridor Protected Area
why: Highway-corridor protected area adjoining Mount Robson Park; no developed campground listed.

name: Mount Terry Fox Park
why: Memorial park on the peak named for Terry Fox above Valemount; viewpoint and rough hiking, no campground listed.

name: Hamber Park
why: Fortress Lake wilderness park wedged against Jasper National Park, reached on foot or by floatplane only.

name: Foster Arm Protected Area
why: Kinbasket Reservoir arm protected for wildlife habitat; no road access or facilities listed.

name: Mount Assiniboine Park
why: The Matterhorn of the Rockies and Lake Magog core area, reached by a 27 km hike or helicopter from the Banff side.

name: Height of the Rockies Park
why: Wilderness park of 3,000 m peaks and alpine lakes on the Continental Divide south of Kananaskis; no vehicle campground.

name: Dry Gulch Park
why: Twenty-seven reservable sites in dry Douglas-fir country just south of Radium Hot Springs.

name: James Chabot Park
why: Windermere Lake beach and day-use park at Invermere; no camping.

name: Akamina-Kishinena Park
why: Remote BC corner adjoining Waterton and Glacier, reached via the Akamina Pass trail from the Waterton side; wilderness camping only.

name: sw̓iw̓s Park
why: Forty-one sites on the sand spit at Haynes Point, Osoyoos Lake, the most sought-after and quickest-booked campground in BC.
rigNote: No length data. BC Parks page mentions 'Lakeside campsites and privacy' but publishes no vehicle length; camping.bcparks.ca reservation API refused fetch (403), so no per-site pad lengths obtainable. Campendium listing (as Haynes Point) has no max vehicle length logged; reviewers describe the campground as sitting on 'a narrow peninsula' with 'overflow along the road' when full - suggests tight manoeuvring for a 40 ft coach.

name: Inkaneep Park
why: Seven quiet cottonwood-shaded sites on the Okanagan River north of Oliver.
rigNote: Explicitly big-rig-hostile. BC Parks official page: 'Most sites will not accommodate large RVs and 5th wheel trailers' and 'The campground is best suited for tenters and small RVs.' Campendium echoes this and notes only 7 gravel sites. No number published, but a 40 ft Class A should be treated as a no.

name: Johnstone Creek Park
why: Sixteen roadside sites in ponderosa pine on Highway 3 near Rock Creek, an easy overnight stop.
rigNote: No length data. BC Parks page describes only 'camping in a quiet, forested creek side setting'; reservation API refused fetch (403). Campendium 'Longest Vehicle Reported' is blank; reviewers mention 'pull through sites available' and use nearby Kettle River for the dump station and showers. Nothing credible found.

name: Conkle Lake Park
why: Thirty-four sites on a clear warm lake reached by 26 km of gravel, known for swimming and rainbow trout.
rigNote: Explicitly big-rig-hostile - do not attempt. BC Parks official page on the two access roads: 'These roads are unsuitable for motorhomes, vehicles towing trailers or low-clearance vehicles.' Access is 16 km of narrow winding forest service road from Hwy 33 or 26 km from Hwy 3 (Camping & RVing BC describes the Hwy 3 route as 25 km of maintained gravel, ~40 minutes). Campground has ~33-36 sites. A 40 ft coach towing a pickup should not go in.

name: Vaseux Lake Park
why: Twelve sites beside a birding hotspot lake under the Vaseux cliffs, home to California bighorn sheep.
rigNote: No length data. BC Parks page has no camping specifications at all; reservation API refused fetch (403). Campendium 'Longest Vehicle Reported' is blank, no hookups, and the only rig-relevant comments concern highway noise (park is immediately beside Hwy 97). Nothing credible found.

name: Rock Creek Park
why: Small park at the Kettle River and Rock Creek confluence; no campground listed by BC Parks.

name: Kettle River Recreation Area
why: 114 reservable sites in cottonwood and ponderosa flats on the Kettle River, with tubing and the Kettle Valley Rail Trail.
rigNote: No credible number. BC Parks page gives no length; reservation API refused fetch (403). Campendium shows 'longest vehicle reported' = 13 ft, but that is a single 2018 small-rig entry and is clearly not a site limit - other reviewers describe 'Sites were large and roomy, private or in the open' and a 'Big easy back in site' with a travel trailer (2025). Deliberately left null rather than propagate the misleading 13 ft.

name: sx̌ʷəx̌ʷnitkʷ Park
why: Thirty-one sites at Okanagan Falls on the Okanagan River channel, walking distance to town.
rigNote: BC Parks page gives no length (campground map PDF only); Camping & RVing BC lists 25 sites with 'RV Sites Available'. Campendium longest vehicle reported = 35 ft (fifth-wheel, 'Beautiful, well cared for', ample spacing) and a reviewer notes 'some are large enough for big rigs'. No hookups. 40 ft unverified.

name: Keremeos Columns Park
why: Hexagonal basalt columns above Keremeos; the approach crosses private land and there are no facilities.

name: Cathedral Park
why: Alpine plateau of turquoise lakes and quartz rock formations south of Keremeos, core area reached by 4x4 shuttle or a long climb.

name: Nickel Plate Park
why: High plateau lake above Apex Mountain used for fishing and Nordic skiing; no developed campground listed.

name: Stemwinder Park
why: Twenty-seven reservable sites on the Similkameen River on Highway 3 west of Hedley.

name: Bromley Rock Park
why: Seventeen sites under a big cliff on a deep green Similkameen swimming hole east of Princeton.

name: Skaha Bluffs Park
why: One of Canada's premier sport-climbing crags in gneiss bluffs above Skaha Lake; day use only.

name: Jewel Lake Park
why: Twenty-six first-come sites on a small mountain lake north of Greenwood, stocked for rainbow trout.

name: Boothman's Oxbow Park
why: Kettle River oxbow near Grand Forks protecting riparian habitat; no campground listed.

name: Kickininee Park
why: Three lakeside day-use sites (Kickininee, Soorimpt, Pyramid) on the Okanagan Lake shore south of Penticton.

name: Sun-Oka Beach Park
why: One of the best swimming beaches on Okanagan Lake, day use only, at Summerland.

name: Okanagan Lake Park
why: 175 sites in two campgrounds under planted shade trees on the Okanagan Lake shore near Summerland.

name: Okanagan Mountain Park
why: Rugged fire-regenerated bluff country between Naramata and Kelowna, hiking, horse and boat-in wilderness camping.

name: Myra-Bellevue Park
why: Myra Canyon trestles on the Kettle Valley Rail Trail above Kelowna, a signature Okanagan bike ride.

name: Algonquin Provincial Park
why: Ontario's flagship wilderness park - maple hills, thousands of lakes, legendary canoe routes and roughly 500 electrical car-camping sites along the Highway 60 corridor.

name: Arrowhead Provincial Park
why: Huntsville's year-round park with 175 electrical sites, a sand beach and famous winter skating trail.
rigNote: No number from any tier. Ontario Parks publishes per-site vehicle lengths only inside reservations.ontarioparks.ca, which was not retrievable, and the park page gives none. Positive signals: paved roads throughout, a purpose-built RV area with drive-through sites, seven year-round pull-through sites between the East River and Roe campgrounds, Roe described as large well-drained electric sites, multiple dump stations, 30 amp. Largest rig found in reviews is 28ft, which is a floor not a ceiling. Worth a phone call to 705-789-5105.

name: Bon Echo Provincial Park
why: 100 m Mazinaw Rock with 260+ Indigenous pictographs; 495 car-camping sites, 214 electrical.

name: Bronte Creek Provincial Park
why: Family park around a 50 m deep ravine with 145 electrical sites and heavy interpretive programming.

name: Charleston Lake Provincial Park
why: Canadian Shield family camping park near Gananoque with 235 sites, 122 electrical, and good paddling.
rigNote: No number from any tier - Ontario Parks per-site lengths live only in the blocked reservation system, and Campendium's longest-vehicle-reported field is blank for Shady Ridge and shows only 12ft for Bayside. 236 sites across Bayside, Shady Ridge and Meadowlands; 30 amp, showers, rebuilt easy-access dump station. Hilly, heavily wooded Frontenac Arch terrain - assume tight interior roads until confirmed with the park at 613-659-2065.

name: Earl Rowe Provincial Park
why: Hiking and biking trails plus autumn salmon runs on the Boyne River; 403 sites, 163 electrical.

name: Ferris Provincial Park
why: Pedestrian suspension bridge over the Trent River gorge above Ranney Falls, 163 sites with 40 electrical.

name: Fitzroy Provincial Park
why: Century-old white pines where the Carp meets the Ottawa River; 235 sites, 106 electrical, an hour from Ottawa.

name: Forks of the Credit Provincial Park
why: Day-use park on the Bruce Trail with the Credit River gorge, kettle lake and cataract falls.

name: Frontenac Provincial Park
why: Backcountry-only park: 54 interior sites, 100+ km of trails and canoe routes across 22 lakes.

name: Killbear Provincial Park
why: Rugged Georgian Bay granite shoreline mixed with sand beaches, 886 sites of which 252 are electrical.

name: Komoka Provincial Park
why: Near-urban day-use park on the Thames River west of London, old farmland reverting to meadow and riverside forest.

name: Lake on the Mountain Provincial Park
why: Geological oddity - a spring-fed lake perched 60 m above the Bay of Quinte with no visible source.

name: Mikisew Provincial Park
why: Three shallow sandy beaches on Eagle Lake with 94 electrical sites, dog-friendly and family oriented.

name: Mono Cliffs Provincial Park
why: Day-use Niagara Escarpment park with 30 m cliffs, keyhole canyon and Bruce Trail access.

name: Murphys Point Provincial Park
why: Rideau-country park built around the 1900s Silver Queen mica mine, 157 sites with 47 electrical and 30 pull-throughs.

name: North Beach Provincial Park
why: A quiet kilometre-long sand ribbon on Lake Ontario, day-use alternative to busy Sandbanks.

name: Oastler Lake Provincial Park
why: Small waterfront campground near Parry Sound with 42 electrical sites and panoramic lake views.

name: Oxtongue River - Ragged Falls Provincial Park
why: Short trail to a thundering whitewater cascade just outside Algonquin's west gate - a quick day-use stop.

name: Pinery Provincial Park
why: Rare oak savanna and 10 km of Lake Huron beach with National Geographic top-ten sunsets; 1,010 sites, 474 electrical.

name: Point Farms Provincial Park
why: Bluff-top park north of Goderich with big Lake Huron sunsets; 151 electrical sites and 9 pull-throughs.

name: Port Bruce Provincial Park
why: Free day-use 200 m sand beach on Lake Erie with shallow, clear water.

name: Port Burwell Provincial Park
why: 2.5 km of the finest sand beach on Lake Erie's north shore; 235 sites, 123 electrical.

name: Presqu'ile Provincial Park
why: World-class migration birding spot - 338 recorded species - with 384 campsites including 158 electrical.
rigNote: No official or reservation number - the Ontario Parks camping page lists eight campgrounds (High Bluff ~100 mostly electric sites, Pines all-electric, Maples ~50 non-electric, Lakeside, Trails End almost all electric, Craigs, Hidden Valley, Elmvale) with no lengths, and the reservation system was not retrievable. Campendium's longest camper-reported rig at High Bluff is 29ft; 30 and 50 amp available. High Bluff and Trails End are the loops to ask about.

name: Rideau River Provincial Park
why: Camping on the UNESCO-listed Rideau Waterway near Merrickville; 186 sites, 77 electrical, 16 pull-through.
rigNote: Camper-sourced: Campendium lists a 50ft maximum RV length and its longest camper-reported rig is also 50ft, so a 40ft coach is corroborated as having fit. 186 sites, electric / non-electric / tent, 30 amp and water at select sites, 23-day max stay. No Ontario Parks or reservation-system figure available to promote this to a higher tier.

name: Sandbanks Provincial Park
why: World's largest baymouth barrier dune formation and three of Canada's best beaches; 268 electrical and 56 pull-through sites.

name: Sharbot Lake Provincial Park
why: Two clear lakes with swimming and paddling, 145 sites of which 38 are electrical.
rigNote: No number from any tier. Campendium's listing for The Point campground carries no max-RV-length and no longest-vehicle-reported value; Ontario Parks publishes nothing and reservations.ontarioparks.ca was not retrievable. Small park, three campgrounds, tent camping prominent - no evidence either way that a 40ft coach fits.

name: Silver Lake Provincial Park
why: Compact lakeside park on Highway 7 with 146 sites, 27 electrical - handy overnight between Perth and Kingston.
rigNote: No number from any tier. Ontario Parks' own camping page states the Wesley Campground 'accommodates large trailers' but gives no figure, and the reservation system holding per-site lengths was not retrievable. 100+ treed sites, some electric, one barrier-free site, barrier-free comfort station. A few sites require parking in a nearby lot. Wesley is the loop to ask about for a 40ft coach.

name: Six Mile Lake Provincial Park
why: Muskoka boating-and-fishing park with 223 sites, 55 of them electrical.

name: The Massasauga Provincial Park
why: Boat-access-only backcountry park of Georgian Bay islands and inland lakes, sanctuary for the massasauga rattlesnake.

name: Parc national de la Yamaska
why: Ring of trail and bike path around the Choiniere Reservoir, the Townships' easy family water park.

name: Parc national du Mont-Orford
why: Eastern Townships mountain park with 80+ km of trails, two clear lakes and 400+ serviced and unserviced campsites at Lac-Stukely and Lac-Fraser.

name: Parc national du Mont-Saint-Bruno
why: Day-use biodiversity island near Montreal with five lakes, an orchard and a historic mill - no camping on site.

name: Ausable Point Campground
why: 123 sites on a natural sand Lake Champlain shoreline beside the Ausable Marsh wildlife area.
rigNote: Longest site 40ft in the DEC ReserveAmerica feed, but max TRAILER length is listed at 35ft - the 40ft figure applies to a small number of sites. 120 sites, no pull-throughs, big-rig flag NO, no hookups (water and dump station only). Exactly-40ft site for a 40ft coach means no margin and the toad has to go somewhere else.

name: Bear Mountain State Park
why: Rugged Hudson-side mountain park with the historic Bear Mountain Inn, Perkins Drive and Fort Clinton ruins.

name: Beaverkill Campground
why: 45 sites strung along the famous Beaverkill trout stream under a historic covered bridge.

name: Buck Pond Campground
why: 116 secluded sites with a guarded beach on Lake Kushaqua north of Saranac Lake.

name: Clermont State Historic Site
why: Seven generations of the Livingston family on a riverfront estate with formal gardens and Catskill views.

name: Cranberry Lake Campground
why: 171 sites on one of the largest remote lakes in the Adirondacks with 50 miles of trail nearby.

name: Crown Point Campground
why: 66 sites beside the 1775 fort ruins and lighthouse on Lake Champlain - the page states any size RV fits.
rigNote: Longest site 40ft; 66 sites, big-rig flag YES, no pull-throughs. Listing notes GRASS driveways 'with most accommodating any size RV via back-in driveways' - grass means soft ground risk for a 40ft Class A in wet weather. No hookups; dump station. On the Lake Champlain shore by the bridge to VT.

name: Crown Point State Historic Site
why: Ruins of the 18th-century French and British forts guarding the Lake Champlain narrows.

name: Cumberland Bay State Park
why: Large natural sand beach at Plattsburgh with a four-loop campground on Lake Champlain.
rigNote: Best NY option in this batch. NY State Parks feed gives 50ft max RV / 50ft max trailer across 400+ sites in four loops, described as 'varying pad lengths from 20 to 50 feet, all back-in configuration' - no pull-throughs, and the big-rig flag is NO despite the length. 20 electric sites in Loop 300; water spigots but no water/sewer at sites. Campendium independently lists max length 50ft and tags it 'big rigs'; a 32ft trailer reported easy backing with ~18ft to the next rig. Downside from reviews: parking on grass, packed in, group-heavy, not quiet.

name: Devil's Tombstone Campground
why: 24 primitive sites in Stony Clove Notch, oldest campground in the Catskill Forest Preserve and Devil's Path trailhead.
rigNote: BIG-RIG HOSTILE despite the 40ft code. Only 24 tent/trailer sites, big-rig flag NO, no hookups, no showers (nearest are 8 miles away at North-South Lake), no cell service on any carrier. The campground sits in Stony Clove Notch directly on NY-214, a narrow steep Catskill notch road with rock walls - the approach, not the site, is the limiter for a 40ft coach towing. Seasonal: 15 May to Labor Day.

name: Eagle Point Campground
why: 72 sites on the west shore of Schroon Lake with wilderness trail access; 30-foot limit.

name: Eighth Lake Campground
why: 126 sites between Seventh and Eighth Lakes on the Fulton Chain, strong lake trout fishing.

name: Fahnestock State Park (Clarence Fahnestock)
why: 15,000 acres of Hudson Highlands lakes and trails; 80 campsites take RVs but have no hookups or dump station.
rigNote: Longest site 30ft in the NY State Parks feed; 80 wooded sites, no pull-throughs, big-rig flag NO. Explicitly 'a primitive camping area with no electric, water, or sewer hookups, and NO DUMP STATION' - showers only, Memorial Day to Labor Day. 40ft coach does not fit.

name: Fish Creek Pond Campground
why: Often called the finest Adirondack campground - 355 sandy waterfront sites taking everything from tents to 40-foot RVs.
rigNote: Verified per-site on newyorkstateparks.reserveamerica.com: lengths are coded in 10/20/30/40ft buckets and 40ft is the top bucket (sites 035, 036, 046, 048, 052, 064, 094, 171 among others). 355 sites total (330 bookable units), big-rig flag YES, no pull-throughs, no hookups but a dump station. The largest DEC pool of 40ft sites in this batch - but 40ft is the ceiling, so a 40ft coach is a zero-margin fit and the toad parks elsewhere.

name: Forked Lake Campground
why: Remote trail- and boat-access sites; only three sites take a 20-foot RV, so this is a truck-and-canoe trip.

name: Frontier Town Campground, Equestrian and Day Use Area
why: Newest DEC facility at Exit 29: 13 electric RV sites, 19 equestrian sites and river access - the Adirondack 'gateway hub'.
