rigNote: Newest DEC facility and the only one here with electric at RV sites. Feed gives 40ft max RV / 40ft max trailer, pull-throughs YES, big-rig flag NO. Inventory is the limiter: 77 sites total but only 13 in the Stagecoach RV/Trailer Loop (all with electric pads, fireplaces, nearby water spigots); the 19-site Blacksmith loop is equestrian (50-amp) and Prairie Junction's 45 sites are tent/group. Dump station, no water/sewer at sites. Right off I-87 exit 29.

name: Golden Beach Campground
why: 207 sites on 5,935-acre Raquette Lake - central Adirondack water recreation hub.

name: Harriman State Park
why: Second-largest park in the NY system - 46,000 acres, 31 lakes, 200 miles of trail; tent camping at Beaver Pond.

name: Hudson Highlands State Park Preserve
why: 8,000 acres and 70+ miles of trail including Breakneck Ridge - hiking only, camping prohibited throughout.

name: James Baird State Park
why: 590-acre day-use park off the Taconic Parkway built around a Robert Trent Jones golf course.

name: John Brown Farm State Historic Site
why: Home and grave of abolitionist John Brown, on the plateau just south of Lake Placid village.

name: Kenneth L. Wilson Campground
why: 76 tent and trailer sites ringed by mountains near Woodstock with paddling and Slide Mountain access.
rigNote: Longest site 40ft in the DEC ReserveAmerica feed; 76 sites, no pull-throughs, big-rig flag NO, no hookups (dump station, water spigots nearby sites). 40ft exactly equals the coach with no margin, back-in only.

name: Lake Durant Campground
why: 65 quiet tent and trailer sites with Blue Mountain views near Indian Lake.

name: Lake Eaton Campground
why: 135 tent and trailer sites at Long Lake with boat rentals and a paved loop road good for bikes.
rigNote: Longest site 30ft (max RV 30 / max trailer 30); 135 wooded tent/trailer sites, no pull-throughs, big-rig flag NO, no hookups (dump station only). 40ft coach does not fit.

name: Lake Harris Campground
why: 89 sites (57 on the shoreline) on the headwaters Hudson at Newcomb; takes RVs to 40 feet.
rigNote: Longest site 40ft (max RV 40 / max trailer 40); 89 sites (57 shoreline, 32 set back), no pull-throughs, big-rig flag YES. No hookups; dump station. 40ft is the ceiling - exact fit for the coach, back-in only.

name: Lake Taghkanic State Park
why: Columbia County lake park with two beaches, cabins and cottages; trailer/RV sites listed up to 20 feet.

name: Lincoln Pond Campground
why: 35 sheltered sites with boat rentals and a beach south of Elizabethtown.
rigNote: Longest site 30ft (max RV 30 / max trailer 30); tiny - 35 units of which 24 are developed sites, 10 remote shoreline and 3 island. No pull-throughs, big-rig flag NO, no hookups. 40ft coach does not fit.

name: Little Pond Campground
why: 67 quiet sites around a 13-acre pond with access to Delaware Wild Forest trails.

name: Macomb Reservation State Park
why: Wilderness-feel park on the Salmon River surrounded by state land, with electric and non-electric wooded sites.
rigNote: Confirmed against the agency booking system itself, not just a mirror: newyorkstateparks.reserveamerica.com lists 40ft Back-In sites in all three loops (e.g. 109, 116 in Lower Loop; 301 in Upper Loop; 215 in the Electric loop). 96 campsites plus 2 pavilions. 30-amp electric on select Electric-loop sites; no water or sewer. No pull-throughs, big-rig flag NO. 40ft = zero margin for the coach.

name: Meacham Lake Campground
why: 223 sites on a big undeveloped lake with wide-open views and loons - takes tents through large RVs.
rigNote: Longest site 40ft (max RV 40 / max trailer 40); 214 sites including 4 group camps, no pull-throughs, big-rig flag NO, no hookups. 40ft is the top DEC bucket - exact fit, zero margin, back-in only.

name: Meadowbrook Campground
why: 62 sites four miles from Lake Placid village - the cheapest base for the Olympic venues and High Peaks.
rigNote: Longest site 30ft (max RV 30 / max trailer 30) in the NYS DEC ReserveAmerica feed; 62 sites, no pull-throughs, big-rig flag NO, no hookups. NY DEC codes per-site length in 10/20/30/40ft buckets, so 30 is a genuine ceiling here. 40ft coach does not fit.

name: Mills Norrie State Park (Margaret Lewis Norrie)
why: 1,000 acres of Hudson River parkland with a marina, golf and a campground - RVs welcome but no hookups.
rigNote: Longest site 30ft in the NY State Parks ReserveAmerica feed, but that is the optimistic reading: the newyorkstateparks.reserveamerica.com site list shows sites 003-022 all coded '20 Back-In', and the listing text says the park 'accommodates smaller RVs up to 20 feet with back-in sites only'. 44 tent sites, 6 electric, 3 platform tents, 10 cabins. No pull-throughs, big-rig flag NO. Treat as a 20ft campground; a 40ft coach is out of the question.

name: Minnewaska State Park Preserve
why: Shawangunk white-conglomerate cliffs, sky lakes and waterfalls; camping is tent-only at the Shawangunk Gateway campground.

name: Mongaup Pond Campground
why: 163 sites on the largest body of water in the Catskill Park outside the NYC reservoirs.

name: North-South Lake Campground
why: The biggest and most popular Catskill campground - 219 sites on the escarpment above Kaaterskill Falls.
rigNote: CONFLICT within the reservation data: max RV length is coded 40ft but max TRAILER length is 30ft, and the campground description says it 'accommodates tents and trailers up to 30 feet'. 219 sites across 7 loops, some pull-throughs, big-rig flag NO, no hookups (dump station + water). Plan on 30ft as the practical figure; the 40ft sites are few. Access is via CR-18 from Haines Falls on the Catskill escarpment.

name: Olana State Historic Site
why: Frederic Church's Persian-inspired mansion and designed landscape over the Hudson - the Hudson River School shrine.

name: Paradox Lake Campground
why: 58 hardwood-hill sites with boat rentals on Paradox Lake near Schroon.
rigNote: Feed codes 40ft max RV, but the same listing describes the 58 sites as tent-oriented and sets the big-rig flag to NO; no pull-throughs, no hookups. Treat the 40ft as applying to a handful of sites only. Seasonal 15 May to early September.

name: Point Au Roche State Park
why: Protected sandy beach, mooring field and year-round nature center on Lake Champlain's northwest shore.

name: Putnam Pond Campground
why: 72 sites including nine remote ones - the main jumping-off point for the Pharaoh Lake Wilderness.

name: Rollins Pond Campground
why: Quiet paddler's campground next to Fish Creek with 287 sites sized to 40-foot RVs.
rigNote: Longest site 40ft (DEC's top length bucket); 287 sites, both back-in and pull-through driveways, big-rig flag YES. No hookups; dump station on site. Shares the access road with Fish Creek Pond. 40ft = exact fit, no margin, toad must be dropped.

name: Saranac Lake Islands Campground
why: 87 boat-access island and shoreline sites on Lower Saranac Lake with lock access to four more lakes.

name: Scaroon Manor Campground
why: 60 modern sites on 1,200 feet of Schroon Lake shoreline at Taylor's Point.

name: Sharp Bridge Campground
why: Small 40-site Schroon River campground aimed at day hikes into the eastern High Peaks; 25-foot limit.

name: Staatsburgh State Historic Site
why: Beaux-Arts Gilded Age mansion of Ogden and Ruth Livingston Mills above the Hudson.

name: Taconic State Park - Copake Falls Area
why: Base for Bash Bish Falls and the Copake Iron Works, with about 30 trailer sites taking up to 26 feet.

name: Taconic State Park - Rudd Pond Area
why: 64-acre pond with ground and platform tent sites and a trail system into the Taconic ridge.

name: Taylor Pond Campground
why: Quiet 30-site pond under Catamount Mountain, five of the sites boat-access only.

name: Wilmington Notch Campground
why: 54 sites right on the West Branch Ausable, the classic base for fly fishing and Whiteface.

name: Woodland Valley Campground
why: 69 sites at the foot of Slide Mountain, the Catskills' highest peak, with stream fishing at the door.
rigNote: Longest site 30ft; ~67-69 wooded tent/trailer sites, no pull-throughs, no electric/water/sewer (dump station only). Reached by the narrow dead-end Woodland Valley Road up the Esopus valley - a 40ft coach towing should not attempt it, and no site would take it anyway. Frequent black bear activity; food storage mandatory.

name: Alburgh Dunes State Park
why: One of the longest beaches on Lake Champlain with rare dune and wetland habitat, day use only.

name: Allis State Park
why: Hilltop park on the summit of Bear Hill with a fire-tower lookout over central Vermont; 18 tent/RV sites.
rigNote: Per-site driveway lengths from the Vermont booking system: longest 35ft (T01, T02, T14, T15), then 34ft (T13, T16), 28ft (T07-T10) and 20ft. Tiny hilltop park (~18 tent/RV sites plus lean-tos) so the visible listing is essentially the whole campground; many lean-to and tent sites carry no driveway length at all. No hookups anywhere in the Vermont system. A 40ft coach does not fit.

name: Big Deer State Park
why: Small quiet 22-site campground in the middle of 26,000-acre Groton State Forest.
rigNote: Per-site driveway lengths from the Vermont booking system: longest is T02 at 35ft; eight sites at 34ft (T05, T09, T10, T13, T14, T25, T27, T28), most of the rest at 28ft, two at 20ft. Small Groton State Forest campground (~24 tent/RV sites plus lean-tos), so the visible listing covers nearly the whole park. No hookups anywhere in the Vermont system. A 40ft coach does not fit.

name: Branbury State Park
why: 1,000-foot natural sand beach on Lake Dunmore under the Moosalamoo cliffs; 36 tent/RV sites.

name: Burton Island State Park
why: Car-free island campground reached by the Island Runner ferry, with a full marina and 43 sites.

name: Button Bay State Park
why: Clay 'button' concretions and a bluff over Lake Champlain; 53 tent/RV sites, no hookups.
rigNote: Vermont booking system shows the longest driveways at 35ft - sites T01 and T21 in Loop 1 - then one at 34ft and the rest at 28 or 20ft. ZERO sites at 40ft or more on the visible list. Caveat: the list paginates and only 25 of 71 units were retrievable, so this is the max across the first quarter of the campground. No hookups anywhere in the Vermont system. A 40ft coach does not fit.

name: Camel's Hump State Park
why: Vermont's iconic undeveloped summit - trail-only access with primitive camping and Green Mountain Club shelters.

name: Crystal Lake State Park
why: Historic granite bathhouse and nearly a mile of beach on a three-mile glacial lake in the Northeast Kingdom.

name: D.A.R. State Park
why: Small Champlain-shore campground opposite Fort Ticonderoga, 47 tent/RV sites and good birding.
rigNote: Vermont booking system shows the longest driveways at 35ft on sites T01 and T17, both PULL-THROUGH - the only pull-throughs in the park and the most usable sites for a larger rig. Everything else is 20-30ft, and zero sites reach 40ft. Site list paginates so only the first 25 units were retrievable. No hookups anywhere in the Vermont system. A 40ft coach does not fit.

name: Elmore State Park
why: 'Beauty Spot of Vermont' - 219-acre lake, sand beach and a fire-tower summit hike; 44 tent/RV sites, no hookups.
rigNote: SINGLE-SITE OUTLIER. Vermont's own booking system lists per-site driveway lengths and exactly ONE site reaches 45ft: T39. The rest of the campground is 16-34ft (T34 at 34ft and T35 at 30ft are next longest; most tent/RV sites are 23 or 28ft). So the park is bookable for a 40ft coach only if T39 is free, otherwise it is a sub-35ft campground. As with every Vermont state park, there are NO electric, water or sewer hookups anywhere in the system.

name: Grand Isle State Park
why: Most-visited campground in the Vermont system - 115 tent/RV sites on 4,150 feet of Lake Champlain shore, no hookups.

name: Green River Reservoir State Park
why: Nineteen miles of undeveloped shoreline with 27 boat-access-only paddle-in sites and no potable water.

name: Kamp Kill Kare State Park
why: Old resort point at the tip of St. Albans Point and the ferry landing for Burton Island.

name: Kettle Pond State Park
why: Undeveloped Groton pond with lean-to-only group camping and 17+ miles of connecting trail.

name: Kingsland Bay State Park
why: Quiet Lake Champlain bay with lawns, cliffs and a historic stone house, popular for paddling and events.

name: Knight Point State Park
why: Day-use point on North Hero with the largest undisturbed cobble shoreline on Lake Champlain.

name: Lake Carmi State Park
why: Vermont's fourth-largest natural lake with 138 tent/RV sites and a rare peat bog boardwalk, no hookups.
rigNote: SINGLE-SITE OUTLIER. Vermont's booking system shows exactly one 40ft driveway - site T010 - with the typical range 15-35ft and most sites 20-30ft. The park is large (138 campsites, 35 lean-tos, 2 cabins) and the site list paginates at 25 rows, so there may be another long site not visible, but nothing corroborates anything above 40ft. Even at T010 a 40ft coach is a zero-margin fit, and there are NO hookups anywhere in the Vermont system.

name: Little River State Park
why: Central Vermont's largest campground on Waterbury Reservoir - 81 tent/RV sites, dump station but no hookups.

name: Mount Philo State Park
why: Vermont's first state park (1924) with a famous Champlain Valley overlook - the steep camp road is not recommended for trailers.

name: New Discovery State Park
why: Groton's north-end campground with 38 tent/RV sites plus horse-camping sites and Osmore Pond remote sites.
rigNote: CONFLICT within the reservation data, resolved upward. Campflare's mirror of the Vermont ReserveAmerica feed reports a 45ft maximum site and states the campground 'can accommodate RVs up to 45 feet depending on the site'; the vtstateparks-visit.com site list paginates at 25 rows and the only retrievable page showed 20/28/30/34ft, so the 45ft site sits further into the list. The same mirror was exactly right about Elmore's single 45ft site (T39), which is why I trust it here - but treat 45ft as one or two sites in an otherwise 20-34ft campground. Groton State Forest; no hookups anywhere in the Vermont system.

name: Niquette Bay State Park
why: Day-use trail park climbing two ridges over Malletts Bay with panoramic lake and Green Mountain views.

name: North Hero State Park
why: 399-acre floodplain forest and swimming access on the islands; camping is no longer permitted here.

name: Ricker Pond State Park
why: Groton State Forest pond camping with 26 tent/RV sites, cabins and cottages and a boat launch.
rigNote: Vermont feed max 35ft, but the agency site list is materially smaller: the longest driveway visible is 28ft (T13, T14, T17), with T02/T04/T05/T24 at 20ft and most units being lean-tos, cabins and cottages with no driveway length at all. Plan on ~28ft. Groton State Forest; no hookups anywhere in the Vermont system. A 40ft coach does not fit.

name: Sand Bar State Park
why: Vermont's busiest day-use park - 2,000 feet of shallow warm beach on the causeway to the islands.

name: Seyon Lodge State Park
why: Whole-lodge rental on Noyes Pond, Vermont's only public fly-fishing-only water - no campsites.

name: Silver Lake State Park
why: Sandy swimming beach at Barnard with 39 tent/RV sites, no hookups.

name: Smugglers' Notch State Park
why: Campground in the notch below 1,000-foot cliffs; the park itself says very few sites can take an RV and the notch road is narrow.

name: Stillwater State Park
why: Lake Groton beach campground with 56 tent/RV sites, showers and a dump station but no hookups.
rigNote: Vermont feed max 35ft; the agency site list (page 1 of 76 units) tops out at 34ft on site T05, with T14/T15 at 30ft and the bulk of the loop at 20 or 28ft. 59 tent/RV sites in Groton State Forest. No hookups anywhere in the Vermont system. A 40ft coach does not fit.

name: Underhill State Park
why: Walk-in-only camping at the western trailheads for Mount Mansfield's summit ridge.

name: Crawford Notch State Park
why: 5,775 acres of the great notch - Arethusa Falls, the Willey House and the 36-site Dry River campground, no hookups.

name: Echo Lake State Park
why: Small beach under White Horse Ledge with the trail link to Cathedral Ledge, minutes from North Conway.

name: Ellacoya State Park
why: 37 three-way full-hookup RV sites on a Lake Winnipesaukee beach with Ossipee and Sandwich range views.

name: Forest Lake State Park
why: 397 acres with a 200-foot sand beach at Dalton, one of the oldest day-use parks in the state.

name: Franconia Notch State Park
why: Flume Gorge, Echo Lake and Cannon Mountain; Lafayette Place is tent-only but the Cannon RV Park has 7 full-hookup sites.
rigNote: SMALLEST IN THIS BATCH. Camping here is Lafayette Place Campground: longest site 28ft (max RV 28 / max trailer 28), 97 wooded sites, no pull-throughs, big-rig flag NO, no hookups and no dump station. nhstateparks.org calls it '97 wooded TENT sites' and points RVs to the separate Cannon RV Park (parking-lot style, no hookups) instead. A 40ft coach cannot camp at Lafayette Place.

name: Jericho Mountain State Park
why: 75+ miles of OHRV trail around Jericho Lake with 9 RV sites - the obvious place to unload the 4x4.
rigNote: Only park in this batch with real room. NH ReserveAmerica feed gives 60ft max RV / 60ft max trailer, pull-throughs YES, big-rig flag YES. Caveat on scale: the whole campground is 20 sites and only NINE are RV sites (rest are 5 cabins, 4 tent sites, 2 Adirondack shelters), added as a trial RV program - so capability is real but inventory is tiny and books out. No hookups and no dump station on site. OHRV park with 75mi of trails, so expect machine noise.

name: Madison Boulder Natural Area
why: One of the largest glacial erratics in North America - 83 feet long and over 5,000 tons.

name: Milan Hill State Park
why: Fire-tower views to Maine and Canada with tent platforms and yurts - no RV hookups.

name: Mollidgewock State Park
why: 44 primitive riverside tent sites on the Androscoggin below Errol - paddling and moose-watching country.

name: Moose Brook State Park
why: 59 sites at Gorham with mountain biking, swimming and the Presidentials and Randolph range at the door; no hookups.
rigNote: Longest site 40ft (max RV 40 / max trailer 40) in the NH ReserveAmerica feed; 56-59 sites across wooded loops, no pull-throughs, big-rig flag NO. nhstateparks.org confirms no hookups AND no dump station. 40ft is exactly the coach length with zero margin, back-in only, and the toad must be dropped elsewhere - marginal at best.

name: Mt. Washington State Park
why: The 6,288-foot summit itself - Sherman Adams center, observatory and Tip-Top House, reached by auto road or cog.

name: Umbagog Lake State Park
why: Base camp with 27 water-and-electric sites plus 33 remote boat-in sites on a wild moose-and-loon lake.

name: Weeks State Park
why: John Wingate Weeks' Mount Prospect estate and stone tower, with a summit auto road and big Presidential views.

name: Wellington State Park
why: Largest freshwater swimming beach in the NH park system, on Newfound Lake.

name: Wentworth State Park
why: 50-acre day-use beach on Lake Wentworth at Wolfeboro.

name: White Lake State Park
why: Roughly 200 wooded sites around a clear glacial lake in a pitch-pine stand; dump station but no hookups.
rigNote: Longest site 38ft in the NH State Parks ReserveAmerica feed; ~200 wooded sites, no pull-throughs, no electric/water/sewer at sites (dump station and coin showers only). 38ft is under the coach's 40ft. Campendium's longest reported rig is 21ft and a reviewer with a 26ft trailer called site 8 'a very tight fit', advising anything bigger than a large pop-up stick to the perimeter roads because 'the inner roads are very narrow with huge old pine trees to navigate through.' Also: no pets anywhere in the park.

name: Clarksburg State Park
why: 46 wooded sites by Mauserts Pond on the Vermont line; small RVs and pop-ups only, no hookups or dump station.
rigNote: Longest site 35ft in the MA DCR ReserveAmerica feed; 46 wooded sites plus 4 yurts, no pull-throughs, big-rig flag NO. mass.gov's own page is blunter: 'Campsites accommodate tents, pop-up trailer and small RV. No electrical hook up or dump station.' 40ft coach does not fit.

name: Mount Greylock State Reservation
why: Highest point in Massachusetts with 90-mile views; vehicles over 22 feet are barred from the summit road and Sperry camping is hike-in.

name: Mount Washington State Forest
why: South Taconic ridge walking to Alander Mountain in the far southwest corner; backcountry camping (currently closed).

name: October Mountain State Forest
why: Largest state forest in Massachusetts, with a tent-and-RV campground and yurts near Lee and Tanglewood; no electrical hookups.
rigNote: OUTLIER WARNING - do not read 50ft as big-rig capability. The MA DCR ReserveAmerica feed lists a 50ft maximum somewhere in the campground, but the same listing states only EIGHT sites take RVs up to 34ft, out of 44 wooded sites plus 3 yurts, and the big-rig flag is NO. Campendium puts the park max at 35ft and the longest rig anyone has reported here at 24ft, with reviewers saying it is 'mostly for tenters', the RV loop is 11 small sites very close together, and 'large RVs might have a hard time getting here.' Treat this as a sub-35ft campground; a 40ft coach plus toad is not realistic. No hookups; dump station on site.

name: Pittsfield State Forest
why: 11,000 acres with Berry Pond, azalea fields and 30 miles of trail; 38 rustic sites in three small campgrounds.

name: Savoy Mountain State Forest
why: Upland forest with 50+ miles of trail, Tannery Falls and log cabins beside a tent campground.

name: Wahconah Falls State Park
why: A 40-foot falls a short walk from the car in Dalton - easy Berkshires waterfall stop.

name: American Legion State Forest
why: 30 RV/tent sites on the Wild and Scenic West Branch of the Farmington - tubing, trout and whitewater.
rigNote: Austin F. Hawes Memorial Campground. Longest site 35ft (max RV 35 / max trailer 35); only 30 tent/RV sites plus 6 cabins, some pull-throughs, big-rig flag NO. No hookups; potable water and dump station shared. Small forest-road campground along the West Branch Farmington; 40ft coach does not fit.

name: Black Rock State Park
why: Rare Connecticut campground with electric and water hookups - 30 RV/tent sites plus swimming and Mattatuck trail access.
rigNote: Longest site 35ft (max RV 35 / max trailer 35) in the CT DEEP ReserveAmerica feed mirrored on Campflare; 78 sites plus 4 rustic cabins, some pull-through driveways, but the feed's big-rig-friendly flag is NO. No hookups today (potable water taps + dump station); electric/water is being added to sites 24, 26 and 28-35 effective 22 Jun 2026 per the same feed. 35ft is a hard ceiling - a 40ft coach does not fit any site here, and there is no site long enough to keep the toad hitched.

name: Burr Pond State Park
why: Site of the world's first condensed milk factory, now a swimming and paddling pond with a loop trail.

name: Dennis Hill State Park
why: Summit pavilion of a former estate at 1,627 feet, looking to Greylock and the Green Mountains.

name: Haystack Mountain State Park
why: 34-foot stone summit tower at Norfolk with views into the Berkshires and Green Mountains.

name: Housatonic Meadows State Park
why: 61 riverside sites beside a two-mile fly-fishing-only stretch of the Housatonic.
rigNote: Longest site 35ft (max RV 35 / max trailer 35); 61 sites plus 4 rustic cabins, some pull-through driveways, big-rig flag NO. No hookups - potable water, dishwashing, dump station only. Campground sits in the narrow Housatonic river corridor off US-7. 40ft coach does not fit.

name: Kent Falls State Park
why: Water cascading 250 feet to the Housatonic past a covered bridge - Connecticut's signature waterfall day trip.

name: Kettletown State Park
why: 55 RV/tent sites over Lake Zoar with six miles of trail; posted maximum RV length is 28 feet.

name: Lake Waramaug State Park
why: 76 RV/tent sites on one of the most picturesque lakes in the state, spectacular in foliage season.
rigNote: Longest site 35ft (max RV 35 / max trailer 35); 76 tent/RV sites plus 6 rustic cabins, ALL back-in, no pull-throughs, big-rig flag NO. No electric/water/sewer at sites; dump station and bathhouses only. Same 35ft ceiling as every other CT DEEP campground checked - the 40ft coach does not fit.

name: Macedonia Brook State Park
why: 51 rustic tent/RV sites with no water or flush toilets, and 10 miles of ridge trail over the Taconics and Catskills.

name: Mount Tom State Park
why: One-mile tower trail to a 34-foot stone tower with one of the best views in Connecticut, plus a swimming pond.

name: Peoples State Forest
why: Old-growth pine stands and Farmington River overlooks across the river from the Legion campground.

name: Squantz Pond State Park
why: Rare stretch of public shoreline on the otherwise private Candlewood Lake system.

name: Talcott Mountain State Park
why: Heublein Tower on a traprock ridge with 360-degree views across the Farmington Valley.

name: Topsmead State Forest
why: English Tudor summer estate with formal gardens and grassland birding right outside Litchfield.

name: Wadsworth Falls State Park
why: 4.5 miles of easy trail to a broad namesake waterfall near Middletown.

name: Camden Hills State Park
why: Mount Battie's auto road over Penobscot Bay with a 107-site campground - one of only six Maine parks with water and electric hookups.

name: Holbrook Island Sanctuary State Park
why: Coastal wildlife sanctuary on Penobscot Bay kept deliberately undeveloped; day use only, no camping anywhere in the park.

name: Lake St. George State Park
why: Spring-fed clear lake on Route 3 with about 40 sites sized from pop-ups to over-35-foot rigs.
rigNote: Best big-rig option in this batch. Maine BPL per-site GIS data gives site 6 as '50+ ft' and site 7 as 50ft, with NINETEEN sites rated 40ft or more (1-7, 11, 13, 15, 19, 23-30). Campendium is more conservative at 35ft and the longest rig actually reported there is only 19ft, but that reflects who visits, not the pads. Reviewers note the middle-section sites are the larger ones and 'many work as pull throughs'; waterfront and wooded sites are more uneven. No hookups.

name: Lamoine State Park
why: 62 quiet shorefront sites on Frenchman Bay across from Acadia - the practical big-rig base for Bar Harbor.
rigNote: Maine BPL publishes per-site maximum camper length in its own campground GIS layer. Longest sites are 1, 2 and 3 (30x70ft pads, 50ft max) and site 33 (60x80ft, 50ft max); site 32 is 40ft. Everything else is 20-35ft, so the 40ft+ inventory is FIVE sites out of ~38. No hookups. Campendium lists the park max as 40ft and reviewers warn about low-hanging branches and tight backing on the lower sites - a 27ft fifth wheel called it 'a little difficult'. Book one of 1/2/3/32/33 or do not come.

name: Warren Island State Park
why: Twelve spruce-shaded sites on an island off Islesboro - you need your own boat to get there.

name: Seaquest State Park
why: Forested camp across SR-504 from the Mount St. Helens Visitor Center and the main approach to the volcano.

name: Pearrygin Lake State Park
why: Warm swimming lake in the Methow Valley just outside Winthrop, with big open hookup loops.

name: Spring Creek Hatchery State Park
why: Small Columbia River day-use site at a working salmon hatchery near White Salmon, popular with windsurfers.

name: Cape Disappointment State Park
why: Two lighthouses, the Lewis and Clark Interpretive Center and old coastal artillery batteries where the Columbia meets the Pacific.

name: Bogachiel State Park
why: Small rainforest camp on the Bogachiel River, the closest state park to Forks and the Hoh.

name: Fort Columbia State Park
why: Intact turn-of-the-century coast artillery post above the Columbia River mouth, with vacation-house rentals.

name: Pacific Pines State Park
why: Undeveloped day-use beach approach on the Long Beach Peninsula at Ocean Park.

name: Doug's Beach State Park
why: Bare-bones Columbia Gorge day-use site that is one of the classic east-end windsurfing launches.

name: Lewis and Clark State Park
why: One of the last stands of old-growth lowland forest in the Cowlitz valley, with CCC-era buildings.
rigNote: 'Maximum site length is 60 feet (may have limited availability)' - this is WA State Parks' own wording carried by two independent third-party mirrors (stateparks.com and camping-usa.com), but the current parks.wa.gov page omits it. 8 full-hookup, 24 standard, 5 primitive equestrian, 1 hiker/biker site.

name: Leadbetter Point State Park
why: Dune, marsh and mudflat trails at the north tip of the Long Beach Peninsula, a major shorebird and snowy plover site.

name: Jackson House State Park Heritage Site
why: Restored 1845 pioneer cabin, the first American home north of the Columbia.

name: Beacon Rock State Park
why: 848-foot basalt monolith with a switchbacked handrail trail, plus Hamilton Mountain and a big Gorge trail network.
rigNote: Woodard Creek Campground accommodates 'RVs and combinations of 40 feet or less in length' - note this is the RV PLUS TOWED combination, so a 40 ft coach towing a pickup exceeds the stated limit and would have to drop the toad. Upper Campground and Equestrian Camp state no limit.

name: Columbia Hills Historical State Park
why: Temani Pesh-wa petroglyphs and Tsagaglalal 'She Who Watches', with Horsethief Lake and spring wildflowers.
rigNote: CONFLICT, conservative figure used: reservation-derived listing for Horsethief Lake says '10 sites can accommodate RVs and trailers between 20 and 35 feet', while the stateparks.com mirror of older WA Parks text claims 60 ft. Both are tier-3 sources; the 35 ft figure fits the campground's actual size (4 standard, 8 partial-hookup, 4 walk-in, 2 hiker/biker). Official parks.wa.gov page publishes no figure. Treat as unsuitable for a 40 ft coach until confirmed by phone (509-773-3145).

name: Sequim Bay State Park
why: Sheltered bay camp in the Olympic rain shadow, on the Olympic Discovery Trail east of Port Angeles.

name: Conconully State Park
why: Quiet reservoir camp in the Okanogan highlands, a short drive over the hill from the Methow.
rigNote: Park page: 'Maximum site length is 75 feet (limited availability).' Comfortable for a 40 ft coach.

name: Reed Island State Park
why: Boat-in only Columbia River island with primitive sites and sandy beaches.

name: Ike Kinswa State Park
why: Big hookup campground on Mayfield Lake with warm-water fishing and swimming.
rigNote: Park page: 'Maximum site length is 60 feet, not all sites achieve the maximum length.'

name: Willie Keil's Grave State Park Heritage Site
why: Roadside heritage site marking the Oregon Trail grave of a boy carried west in a lead-lined coffin.

name: Fort Townsend Historical State Park
why: Quiet second-growth forest camp on the site of an 1856 Army post above Port Townsend Bay.
rigNote: Park page: 'Maximum site length is 40 feet, with limited availability.' Exactly at the coach's length with zero margin and few such sites - the towed pickup will not fit on the pad.

name: Anderson Lake State Park
why: Day-use lake and rolling trails on the Quimper Peninsula; the lake often closes for toxic algae.

name: Paradise Point State Park
why: Convenient I-5 overnight stop on the East Fork Lewis River north of Vancouver.
rigNote: Park page: 'Maximum site length is 40 feet (limited availability).' Exactly at the coach's length with zero margin and few such sites.

name: Lime Kiln Point State Park
why: The best shore-based orca-watching spot in the country, with a working lighthouse on San Juan Island.

name: Fort Worden Historical State Park
why: Sprawling former Army post turned campus at Point Wilson, with batteries, a marine science center and beachfront sites.
rigNote: Park page: 'Maximum site length is 75 feet with limited availability', applying to both the Beach Campground (full hookup) and Upper Forest Campground (partial hookup). Comfortable for a 40 ft coach.

name: Grayland Beach State Park
why: Full-hookup loops tucked in shore pine right behind the dunes on the south Grays Harbor coast.
rigNote: Park page: 'Maximum site length is 60 feet with limited availability' and 'Campsites are large, paved driveways that will accommodate larger RVs.' CONFLICT: campsitephotos claims 40 ft; the official agency figure is the higher tier and is used here.

name: Rainbow Falls State Park
why: Old-growth grove and a low waterfall on the Chehalis River, with CCC-built stone work.
rigNote: Park page: 'Maximum site length is 60 feet (limited availability).'

name: Maryhill State Park
why: Grassy full-hookup riverfront camp on the Columbia below the Maryhill Museum, hot and windy in summer.

name: Fort Ebey State Park
why: WWII gun battery on the Whidbey bluff with prairie, kettle-hole lake and singletrack mountain-bike trails.
rigNote: CONFLICT: reservation-derived listing says '43 sites can accommodate RVs and trailers between 15 and 45 feet'; the stateparks.com mirror claims an implausible 100 ft and is not trusted. Official parks.wa.gov page publishes no figure. Camper reports confirm 'some sites are very large and can accommodate the largest RVs' but warn 'the roads can be a little tight and there are lots of trees trying to grab your rig' - expect overhead branch clearance issues for a 40 ft Class A. No dump station.

name: Alta Lake State Park
why: Warm desert lake camp near Pateros, ringed by ponderosa and post-fire hillsides.
rigNote: Park page: 'maximum site length is 38 feet', applying to standard, partial-hookup and the two group sites. Just under the coach's 40 ft - not usable.

name: Goldendale Observatory State Park Heritage Site
why: Public observatory with a large amateur-built reflector under some of the darkest skies in the Gorge.

name: Twenty-Five Mile Creek State Park
why: Marina and camp far up the south shore of Lake Chelan, the jumping-off point for the upper lake.
rigNote: Big-rig hostile: 'Maximum site length is 30 feet (may have limited availability)' plus 'Access for larger recreational vehicles is limited' at this older campground - confirmed at 30 ft by two independent mirrors of WA State Parks text. Official parks.wa.gov page publishes no figure. Not usable by a 40 ft coach.

name: Fort Flagler Historical State Park
why: Bluff-top artillery fort at the tip of Marrowstone Island with beach camping and long tidal spits.
rigNote: 'Maximum site length is 50 feet (may have limited availability)' for the Lower Campground, corroborated by a second third-party source also giving 'up to 50 feet'. Official parks.wa.gov page describes Lower Campground sites as 'level and spacious' with standard, partial and full hookups but publishes no number. Reservations essential April-October.

name: Mystery Bay State Park
why: Small day-use moorage park on Marrowstone Island's protected bay.

name: Kinney Point State Park Property
why: Undeveloped water-access-only point at the south end of Marrowstone Island with Cascadia Marine Trail sites.

name: Twin Harbors State Park
why: Classic old Washington coast campground in the dunes south of Westport, walk-over access to miles of beach.
rigNote: Big-rig hostile: park page states 'Hookup sites are small and close together; maximum site length is 35 feet with limited availability. Larger RV units may have difficulty.' Not usable by a 40 ft coach.

name: Joseph Whidbey State Park
why: Day-use beach and meadow trails on the west side of Whidbey near Oak Harbor.

name: Turn Island Marine State Park
why: Boat-in island park just off San Juan Island with primitive shoreline sites.

name: Nisqually State Park
why: Washington's newest state park, day-use trails at the Mashel and Nisqually river confluence.

name: Posey Island State Park
why: One-acre kayak-in islet north of Roche Harbor, Cascadia Marine Trail only.

name: Fort Casey Historical State Park
why: Admiralty Head lighthouse and disappearing gun batteries beside the Coupeville ferry landing.

name: Battle Ground Lake State Park
why: Spring-fed crater lake in a forested basin north of Vancouver, popular for swimming and trout.

name: Bottle Beach State Park
why: Grays Harbor mudflat park with viewing platforms; one of the best spring shorebird migration stops on the coast.

name: Federation Forest State Park
why: Preserved old-growth on the White River along SR-410 with an interpretive center and easy loop trails.

name: Westport Light State Park
why: Paved Dune Trail from Westport to the tallest lighthouse in Washington.

name: Spencer Spit State Park
why: Lopez Island park built around a driftwood sand spit and lagoon, reachable only by ferry.

name: Dosewallips State Park
why: Where the Dosewallips River meets Hood Canal - elk, oyster and clam beaches, and hookup sites.

name: Jones Island Marine State Park
why: Boat-in San Juans favourite with tame deer, mooring buoys and a marine-trail camp.

name: Blind Island Marine State Park
why: Tiny treeless islet in Shaw Island's Blind Bay, water access only.

name: Pleasant Harbor State Park Property
why: Small Hood Canal moorage float with no upland facilities.

name: Stuart Island Marine State Park
why: Remote boat-in park at the northwest edge of the San Juans, hiking to Turn Point lighthouse.

name: James Island Marine State Park
why: Steep little boat-in island off Decatur with exposed campsites and strong currents.

name: Shine Tidelands State Park
why: Undeveloped shellfish beach at the west end of the Hood Canal Bridge.

name: Triton Cove State Park
why: Small Hood Canal day-use park and boat launch on US-101.

name: Bridgeport State Park
why: Irrigated green oasis on Rufus Woods Lake below Chief Joseph Dam, with odd volcanic 'haystack' rocks.

name: Lake Chelan State Park
why: Busy lakefront camp on the south shore of Lake Chelan with swimming and boat launch.

name: Deception Pass State Park
why: Washington's most-visited state park - the 1935 bridge over a tidal race, plus forest, lakes and headland trails.

name: Kitsap Memorial State Park
why: Small Hood Canal park just north of the bridge with a bluff-top lawn and beach stairs.

name: Scenic Beach State Park
why: Rhododendron gardens and an oyster beach with a straight-on view of the Olympics across Hood Canal.

name: Brooks Memorial State Park
why: Pine-forest camp at 3,000 feet on US-97 north of Goldendale, a cool escape from the Columbia.

name: Millersylvania State Park
why: Deep Lake CCC park south of Olympia with heavy old-growth fir and a mile-long fitness trail.

name: Fort Simcoe Historical State Park
why: Restored 1856 Army post with original officers' quarters on the Yakama Reservation at Mool Mool spring.

name: Obstruction Pass State Park
why: Half-mile hike-in to pebble-beach campsites on the south shore of Orcas Island.

name: Moran State Park
why: Orcas Island's 5,200-acre core - Mount Constitution's stone tower, five lakes and 38 miles of trail.

name: Doe Island Marine State Park
why: Six-acre boat-in island off the southeast shore of Orcas.

name: Beebe Bridge State Park
why: Columbia River park at Chelan Falls with a swim beach, tennis courts and shaded hookup sites.

name: Nolte State Park
why: Day-use swimming and a 1.4-mile loop around Deep Lake near Enumclaw.

name: Ocean City State Park
why: Dune-backed camp just north of Ocean Shores with direct walk-on beach access.

name: Lake Sylvia State Park
why: Former mill pond turned quiet no-motor lake camp above Montesano.

name: Flaming Geyser State Park
why: Green River day-use park named for a methane seep, with rafting take-outs and river trails.

name: Lake Easton State Park
why: I-90 Cascade-crest camp near the Palouse to Cascades Trail and Lake Easton reservoir.

name: Kanaskat-Palmer State Park
why: Green River Gorge camp used as the put-in for class III whitewater.

name: Clark Island Marine State Park
why: Narrow boat-in island in Rosario Strait with beaches on both sides.

name: Sucia Island Marine State Park
why: Horseshoe of sandstone bays north of Orcas, widely called the best boat-in park in the state.

name: Patos Island Marine State Park
why: Northernmost San Juan park, boat-in camping and the Alden Point lighthouse.

name: Ecola State Park
why: Headland viewpoints over Cannon Beach and Tillamook Rock Light, with the Clatsop Loop and Indian Beach; RVs and trailers are not allowed on the park road.

name: Tolovana Beach State Recreation Site
why: Day-use beach access at the south end of Cannon Beach, the usual walk-up to Haystack Rock.

name: Arcadia Beach State Recreation Site
why: Small US-101 pullout with stairs to a cove beach and tidepools south of Cannon Beach.

name: Hug Point State Recreation Site
why: Beach with a wagon road cut into the headland and a seasonal waterfall, walkable only at low tide.

name: Oswald West State Park
why: Short Falcon Cove trails to Short Sand Beach and the Cape Falcon and Neahkahnie Mountain headlands; the campground is long closed.

name: Del Rey Beach State Recreation Site
why: Straight-shot beach approach north of Gearhart where driving on the sand is allowed.

name: Sunset Beach State Recreation Site
why: Wide vehicle-access beach at the south end of the Clatsop Plains.

name: Nehalem Bay State Park
why: Big flat sand-spit campground between Nehalem Bay and the ocean, with a horse camp and an airstrip.
rigNote: Longest listed site 60 ft but that is HORS08, a pull-through in the horse camp; longest regular campground site is 52 ft (A14), with roughly 18 sites at 40ft+ (A23 51, A17/A19/A25/A27 49, A12/A21 48, A02/A04/A10 47). Only 1 RV permitted per site.

name: Saddle Mountain State Natural Area
why: Steep 2.5-mile climb to the highest point in the northern Coast Range with rare wildflower meadows; small primitive campground.

name: Manhattan Beach State Recreation Site
why: Quiet day-use beach access at Rockaway Beach.

name: Fort Stevens State Park
