why: Seasonal summer dam on the Eel at Benbow, with a campground beside the historic inn.

name: Bodie State Historic Park
why: Arrested-decay gold-rush ghost town at 8,375 feet, reached by three miles of dirt road.

name: Mailliard Redwoods State Natural Reserve
why: Undeveloped second-growth redwood reserve on the Garcia River road.

name: Portola Redwoods State Park
why: Deep basin campground reached by a steep narrow road off Skyline, with old-growth along Peters Creek.

name: Butano State Park
why: Quiet redwood canyon above Pescadero with a small campground and a trail camp.

name: John B. Dewitt Redwoods State Natural Reserve
why: Undeveloped old-growth grove protected on the South Fork Eel.

name: Railtown 1897 State Historic Park
why: Working Sierra Railway roundhouse in Jamestown whose locomotives have appeared in hundreds of films.

name: Trinidad State Beach
why: Cove beach and bluff trails below Trinidad Head.

name: Pigeon Point Light Station State Historic Park
why: One of the tallest lighthouses in America, with a hostel in the keepers' quarters.

name: Columbia State Historic Park
why: Best-preserved Gold Rush town in California, a living-history main street with stagecoaches.

name: Limekiln State Park
why: Redwood canyon on the south Big Sur coast with 1880s lime kilns and a beachside campground.

name: Millerton Lake State Recreation Area
why: Foothill reservoir on the San Joaquin with the old Millerton courthouse moved above the waterline.

name: Bean Hollow State Beach
why: Pebble Beach and a bluff trail with tafoni-pocked sandstone south of Pescadero.

name: Wildcat Hills State Recreation Area
why: Pine-studded escarpment canyons and overlooks above the North Platte Valley, with a nature center; only 12 basic primitive sites and a summit road the park warns is unsuitable for large RVs.

name: Lake Minatare State Recreation Area
why: The Panhandle's largest lake, with 101 Electric Plus sites, shower houses and the 1930s Plains Lighthouse observation tower.
rigNote: Longest site 63ft per the Nebraska Game & Parks / ReserveAmerica data mirrored on Campflare; 121 developed sites (Lake View 52 electric-plus, Butte View 49 electric-plus, West Wind 20 basic) plus scattered primitive and beach camping. NO pull-through sites, so the coach must unhook the pickup and back in. 40ft+ count not exposed.

name: Bridgeport State Recreation Area
why: Five shaded sandpit lakes near Chimney Rock with 72 first-come basic sites and an RV dump/fill station, but no electrical hookups.

name: Box Butte Reservoir State Recreation Area
why: Quiet panhandle reservoir with 60 30/50-amp pads and some of the best birdwatching in western Nebraska.

name: Custer State Park
why: 71,000 acres of Black Hills granite, the Needles Highway and Wildlife Loop bison herd, with nine campgrounds including electric RV sites.

name: Angostura Recreation Area
why: Warm reservoir with the best sandy beaches in South Dakota and 171 sites across four campgrounds, many with electricity.
rigNote: Camper-sourced: Campendium's longest reported rig in Cheyenne campground is a 40ft Class A in site 18, and the listing notes 'most sites are big rig ready' with asphalt pads, pull-throughs, 30 amp, showers and a dump station. SD GFP's park page publishes no lengths (4 campgrounds, 171 sites, 14 cabins) and campsd was not retrievable, so this stays reported tier. Campground sits a few miles off the main road. Add $8 cash park entrance permit on arrival.

name: Bear Butte State Park
why: Sacred laccolith rising off the plains with a steep summit trail and a bison herd; only 15 non-electric first-come sites.

name: Rough Rider State Park
why: Formerly Sully Creek; the badlands horse park just south of Medora at the north trailhead of the Maah Daah Hey, with modern and primitive sites and Little Missouri River access.
rigNote: Whitetail Flats campground: longest site 90ft per the ND state parks reservation data mirrored on Campflare; pull-throughs yes, flagged big-rig friendly, 28 sites (24 single, 4 double), 20/30/50 amp. 40ft+ count not exposed. Corroborated by Campendium - a 39ft fifth wheel stayed in Whitetail Flats. ACCESS NOTE: entry is off a gravel road with a fairly steep hill down to the park entrance, slick after rain. The separate Cedar dry-camping area has a 10ft height restriction.

name: Fort Abraham Lincoln State Park
why: North Dakota's oldest state park, with reconstructed On-A-Slant Mandan earthlodges, Custer's house and 51 modern electric/water campsites.

name: Cross Ranch State Park
why: One of the last free-flowing stretches of the Missouri, with 16 miles of trail, 35 electric sites and an adjoining 5,000-acre bison preserve.
rigNote: Longest site listed at 120ft per ND state parks reservation data mirrored on Campflare - almost certainly one oversized pull-through, not representative. Pull-throughs yes; 35 electric standard sites plus 22 primitive, yurts and cabins. 40ft+ count not exposed. No camper-reported corroboration found, so treat the 120 as the system's longest listing rather than a typical site.

name: Itasca State Park
why: Mississippi headwaters, old-growth red pine and the Wilderness Drive; Minnesota's oldest and busiest park, with large electric campgrounds.

name: La Salle Lake State Recreation Area
why: Minnesota's second-deepest lake on the upper Mississippi, with a newer electric campground ten minutes from Itasca.
rigNote: Longest site 65ft per ReserveMN data mirrored on Campflare; flagged big-rig friendly, NO pull-throughs. 40ft+ count not exposed, but sampled site 19E confirms a 65ft driveway/65ft max RV, so genuine 40ft+ back-in sites exist. Newest MN unit, wide gravel pads.

name: Lake Bemidji State Park
why: Bog boardwalk through lady's-slipper orchids and pitcher plants, plus a sandy Lake Bemidji shoreline and modern campground.
rigNote: Longest site listed at 100ft per ReserveMN data mirrored on Campflare - treat as an outlier value on one long pull-through rather than a typical site. 95 sites, 43 with 30-amp, only 4-5 pull-throughs described as suitable for larger RVs, and the campground is NOT flagged big-rig friendly. 40ft+ count not exposed; realistically the coach is limited to those few pull-throughs.

name: Jay Cooke State Park
why: Swinging bridge over the churning slate gorge of the St. Louis River, with 50 miles of trail just south of Duluth.

name: Moose Lake State Park
why: Home of the Agate and Geological Interpretive Center - the place to learn Lake Superior agates - plus a swimming lake and electric sites.

name: Gooseberry Falls State Park
why: Five waterfalls right off Highway 61 and heavy CCC stonework; the most-visited park on the North Shore.

name: Split Rock Lighthouse State Park
why: The 1910 cliff-top lighthouse and the Little Two Harbors pebble beach; camping here is cart-in and backpack only, so park the coach elsewhere.

name: Tettegouche State Park
why: High Falls of the Baptism River, the Palisade Head cliffs and four inland trout lakes, with a small drive-in campground.

name: George H. Crosby Manitou State Park
why: Rugged backpack-only park where the Manitou River drops through a gorge to Lake Superior - a truck-and-boots day trip.

name: Temperance River State Park
why: River-carved potholes and a narrow slot gorge, plus the Carlton Peak climb; drive-in sites on both sides of Highway 61.

name: Cascade River State Park
why: A staircase of falls in a cedar gorge with Superior Hiking Trail access up Lookout Mountain; small drive-in campground, no hookups.

name: Judge C. R. Magney State Park
why: The Devil's Kettle, where half the Brule River vanishes into a pothole; a rustic drive-in campground and a steep 1.7-mile hike.
rigNote: Longest site 60ft max RV per ReserveMN data mirrored on Campflare, but max TRAILER length is 45ft and the campground has NO pull-throughs and is explicitly flagged not big-rig friendly. 27 drive-in sites, rustic (no hookups), heavily wooded. 40ft+ count not exposed. A 40ft coach plus towed pickup would have to unhook and back in.

name: Grand Portage State Park
why: The 120-foot High Falls of the Pigeon River on the Canadian border - Minnesota's tallest waterfall, day use only.

name: Twin Lakes Campground (Pat Bayle State Forest)
why: Rustic first-come lakeside sites in the hills behind Grand Marais, reached on gravel forest road - small sites, no hookups.
rigNote: No credible length published by MN DNR or any reservation system - state forest campgrounds are rustic, first-come, fee-by-envelope and carry no site dimensions. BIG-RIG HOSTILE: listed as tent/drive-in only, and access is Gunflint Trail 17 mi to South Brule Rd, 6 mi to Lima Mountain Rd, then ~4 mi of unpaved forest road. Not a candidate for a 40ft coach with a toad.

name: Devilfish Lake Campground (Grand Portage State Forest)
why: Tiny rustic campground off the Arrowhead Trail with a boat ramp; a truck-and-tent spot, not coach country.
rigNote: No credible length from any tier. MN DNR describes the Grand Portage State Forest campgrounds as having five or fewer campsites each. BIG-RIG HOSTILE: access is Arrowhead Trail north ~11 mi then ~7 mi east on Esther Lake Road; reviewers report the road up from the North Shore is rough in places and warn low-clearance vehicles. Not viable for a 40ft coach.

name: McFarland Lake Campground (Grand Portage State Forest)
why: A handful of rustic sites at a BWCA entry point on the Arrowhead Trail, with Border Route Trail access.
rigNote: No credible length from any tier; Campendium's longest-vehicle-reported field is blank. First-come, first-served, tent-oriented, five or fewer sites per MN DNR's description of Grand Portage State Forest campgrounds. BIG-RIG HOSTILE: sits at Little John Crossing at the far end of the gravel Arrowhead Trail / McFarland Lake Road. Not viable for a 40ft coach.

name: Mantrap Lake Campground (Paul Bunyan State Forest)
why: Rustic drive-in sites on a clear walleye lake in the Paul Bunyan forest, a cheap alternative to busy Itasca.
rigNote: No length published by MN DNR and not in ReserveMN (first-come, first-served, $17, no hookups, well water and vault toilets). Access is fully paved per multiple Campendium reviewers, and one motorhome owner reports 'many large enough for large RVs' - encouraging but not a number, so left null rather than guessed.

name: Gulch Lake Campground (Paul Bunyan State Forest)
why: Small rustic campground in the Gulch Lakes Recreation Area with hike-in stocked trout lakes.
rigNote: Camper-sourced only: The Dyrt reports the campground takes RVs up to 35ft, which is under the coach's 40ft. ~9 hillside sites plus 3 hike-in. BIG-RIG HOSTILE: access is ~2 mi of East Gulch Forest Road off State Hwy 64; reviewers describe the forest road as challenging for larger RVs and rough when towing. No agency or reservation-system length exists.

name: Indian Lake Campground (Cloquet Valley State Forest)
why: Remote rustic sites on a quiet lake north of Duluth, reached by gravel forest road.

name: Finland Campground and Day Use Area (Finland State Forest)
why: Rustic drive-in sites on the Baptism River - a cheap base for Tettegouche and the Superior Hiking Trail.

name: Eckbeck Campground (Finland State Forest)
why: Rustic riverside sites just off Highway 1 on the Baptism River, first-come only.

name: Big Bay State Park
why: Sandstone sea caves, bluffs and a mile-long boardwalk on Madeline Island - reached by the Bayfield car ferry, so plan the coach carefully.

name: Copper Falls State Park
why: Ancient lava flows, deep gorges and the Doughboys Trail past Copper and Brownstone falls, with CCC log buildings and an electric campground.
rigNote: Longest site 50ft per wisconsin.goingtocamp data mirrored on Campflare; NO pull-throughs and not flagged big-rig friendly. 55 sites: North campground 32 (28 electric, 4 non-electric), South campground 23 non-electric of which 4 are walk-in. North is the only realistic loop for the coach. 40ft+ count not exposed - WI DNR's own page states 'all campsite details, including site lengths, are available on the reservation website' and publishes none itself.

name: Amnicon Falls State Park
why: A chain of falls and rapids on the Douglas Fault crossed by a 1930 bowstring covered bridge; rustic drive-in sites, no hookups.
rigNote: Longest site listed at 50ft per wisconsin.goingtocamp data mirrored on Campflare, but treat with caution: only 36 sites total (one ADA, two walk-in), NO pull-throughs, no electric, and the campground is explicitly flagged NOT big-rig friendly. 40ft+ count not exposed. The 50ft figure is one long site in a small rustic loop, not a general capability.

name: Pattison State Park
why: Big Manitou Falls, at 165 feet the highest waterfall in Wisconsin, plus a swimming beach and a campground with some electric sites.
rigNote: Family campground: longest site 50ft per wisconsin.goingtocamp data mirrored on Campflare; pull-throughs yes but NOT flagged big-rig friendly. 59 family sites, only 18 with 30-amp electric, plus 3 backpack sites 1.6 mi out. 40ft+ count not exposed. WI DNR's camping page publishes no lengths.

name: Peninsula State Park
why: Door County's flagship: over 460 campsites, Eagle Bluff Lighthouse, the Eagle Tower boardwalk and a golf course.

name: Potawatomi State Park
why: Limestone bluffs over Sturgeon Bay and the western terminus of the Ice Age National Scenic Trail.
rigNote: Daisy Field campground: longest site 50ft per wisconsin.goingtocamp data mirrored on Campflare; pull-throughs yes. 123 sites, 40 with electric, plus a 27-site South Daisy Field loop and 4 group sites (two of which take trailers and motorhomes). 40ft+ count not exposed. WI DNR's own camping page publishes no lengths and points to the reservation site.

name: Whitefish Dunes State Park
why: Wisconsin's tallest dunes and the wave-cut cliffs of Cave Point next door; day-use only, no camping.

name: Newport State Park
why: Wisconsin's only wilderness-designated park and an International Dark Sky Park; all 2,300 acres served by hike-in backpack sites.

name: Rock Island State Park
why: No-vehicle island reached by two ferries, with the Pottawatomie Lighthouse and Thordarson's stone boathouse; walk-in sites only.

name: Porcupine Mountains Wilderness State Park
why: 60,000 acres of old-growth with Lake of the Clouds, Summit Peak and the Presque Isle River; the 100-site Union Bay campground has electric sites on Lake Superior.

name: Lake Gogebic State Park
why: Modern campground on the west shore of the UP's largest inland lake, known for walleye and perch.

name: Twin Lakes State Park
why: Warm-water swimming lake on US-45 with a modern campground, a handy stop between the Porkies and the Keweenaw.

name: Bond Falls Scenic Site
why: A 50-foot cascade on the Middle Branch Ontonagon reached by an accessible boardwalk; day use only.

name: Van Riper State Park
why: Sandy Lake Michigamme beach with modern and rustic campgrounds in the heart of Michigan's moose range.
rigNote: Longest site 50ft per midnrreservations mirror; 196 sites (147 modern electric, 40 rustic, 9 group), pull-throughs yes, paved campground roads. Conflict: Campendium states an 85ft max - implausible, preferred the reservation figure. Campendium longest camper-reported rig 30ft; reviewers describe sites very close together and a narrow interior road requiring other campers to move vehicles.

name: Craig Lake State Park
why: Michigan's most remote state park - a rough seven-mile two-track (high-clearance/4x4 recommended) to hike-in sites, rustic cabins and genuine moose habitat.

name: Laughing Whitefish Falls State Park
why: A 100-foot cascade tumbling down a limestone escarpment, a half-mile walk from the lot; day use only.

name: Wagner Falls Scenic Site
why: A short boardwalk to a photogenic multi-tier falls minutes from downtown Munising; day use only.

name: Palms Book State Park
why: Kitch-iti-kipi, the Big Spring - a self-operated observation raft over 40 feet of startlingly clear water; day use only.

name: Indian Lake State Park
why: Two units on Michigan's fourth-largest inland lake with modern electric sites and easy access to Kitch-iti-kipi.

name: Fayette Historic State Park
why: A preserved 1867 iron-smelting company town on Snail Shell Harbor beneath limestone cliffs, with a semi-modern campground.

name: Tahquamenon Falls State Park
why: The 200-foot-wide, root-beer-colored Upper Falls plus the Lower Falls; modern campgrounds at Lower Falls and at the Rivermouth on Whitefish Bay.

name: Muskallonge Lake State Park
why: A narrow strip between warm Muskallonge Lake and the agate-and-driftwood beaches of Lake Superior.
rigNote: Longest site 50ft per midnrreservations mirror; 159 sites, pull-throughs yes. 40ft+ count not exposed, but sampled site 140 shows max RV 40ft on a 45ft driveway, so 40ft-capable sites do exist. Campendium longest camper-reported rig 40ft. Sites 1-80 open, 131-159 wooded/tight; a 27ft trailer reported it was tricky to get in.

name: Brimley State Park
why: Whitefish Bay beach campground with modern sites, handy to the Soo Locks and Point Iroquois Light.
rigNote: Longest site 50ft per midnrreservations mirror; 237 sites, pull-throughs yes, 30 and 50 amp - but NOT flagged big-rig friendly. 40ft+ count not exposed. Campendium agrees 50ft max, longest camper-reported rig 30ft; campground described as condensed and crowded and a 30ft rig needed maneuvering.

name: Straits State Park
why: Bluff campground with head-on Mackinac Bridge views, walking distance to St. Ignace and the island ferries.

name: Wilderness State Park
why: 26 miles of undeveloped Lake Michigan shoreline and dark skies, with modern sites plus newer full-hookup sites.
rigNote: Longest site 50ft (max RV 50 / max trailer 50) per midnrreservations mirror; ~195 sites (East Lakeshore 65, West Lakeshore 71, Pines 99). No pull-throughs. 40ft+ site count not exposed. Renovated East/West Lakeshore loops have concrete pads and are the big-rig loops; a 45ft fifth wheel and a 36ft Class A both report fitting there. Older Pines loop is tight - one 30ft trailer reported being unable to park if the opposite site was occupied.

name: Cheboygan State Park
why: Quiet Duncan Bay campground with Lake Huron beaches and the ruins of the Cheboygan Point light.
rigNote: Longest site 50ft per midnrreservations mirror; 78 modern sites, pull-throughs yes. Conflict: Campendium lists a 60ft policy max - preferred the reservation figure. Only 20-amp power on most sites (shared posts), so A/C on a 40ft coach is doubtful. Access is a ~1 mile gravel entrance road; Campendium longest camper-reported rig only 28ft and sites described as generally small.

name: Aloha State Park
why: Compact, mostly open modern campground on Mullett Lake along the Inland Waterway - easy in-and-out for a big rig.
rigNote: Longest site 50ft per midnrreservations mirror; ~285 sites, mix of full/partial hookup and rustic, 20-50 amp. NO pull-through sites. 40ft+ count not exposed. Campendium longest camper-reported rig only 30ft; single entrance road, drainage/mud issues after rain; paved sites near the entrance are the big-rig option, waterfront sites 195-240 suit rigs under 25ft.

name: Burt Lake State Park
why: A 2,000-foot sand beach at the south end of Burt Lake with a large modern campground.
rigNote: Longest site 50ft per midnrreservations mirror; 300+ sites in east and west loops, pull-throughs yes, flagged big-rig friendly, 30 and 50 amp. Conflict: Campendium states 45ft - preferred the reservation figure. 40ft+ count not exposed. Campendium's longest camper-reported rig is only 18ft, so no camper corroboration of a 40ft+ stay.

name: Petoskey State Park
why: Little Traverse Bay dunes and the best-known beach for hunting Petoskey stones, with two modern campgrounds.
rigNote: EFFECTIVELY CLOSED TO A 40FT COACH. Dunes campground longest site is 25ft max RV per midnrreservations mirror (80 sites, no pull-throughs, explicitly not big-rig friendly); sampled site 19 is max RV 20ft despite a 44ft driveway. Tannery Creek loop (~100 sites) per-site lengths were not retrievable - midnrreservations blocks direct access and no mirror carries it. Lower-tier sources conflict: RVezy lists a 35ft park max, The Dyrt claims up to 50ft, Campendium's longest camper-reported rig is 16ft and reviewers cite narrow winding roads, low branches, and sites 'wide but not deep'. Treat 25ft as the only verified number and assume the park is unusable.

name: Onaway State Park
why: Old-growth hardwoods and glacial granite outcrops on Black Lake; a small, quiet CCC-era park.

name: Young State Park
why: Three modern campgrounds under deep hardwoods on Lake Charlevoix, at the edge of Boyne City.

name: P. H. Hoeft State Park
why: A mile of Lake Huron sand-and-shingle beach with a wooded modern campground on the Sunrise Coast.

name: Keith J. Charters Traverse City State Park
why: In-town modern campground across US-31 from an East Grand Traverse Bay beach - convenient rather than scenic.
rigNote: Longest site 50ft (max RV 50 / max trailer 50) per midnrreservations data mirrored on Campflare; pull-throughs yes, 3 loops ~300-348 sites. Count of 40ft+ sites not exposed (Michigan per-site lengths only visible one site at a time). CAUTION: campground listed as CLOSED for renovation, reopening 1 Apr 2027. Campendium longest camper-reported rig 39ft; reviewers call roads narrow with 100-120 degree turns, hard over 35ft.

name: Interlochen State Park
why: Michigan's first state park: virgin white pines between Duck and Green lakes, next to the Interlochen arts campus.
rigNote: Longest site 50ft (max RV 50 / max trailer 50) per midnrreservations mirror; Duck Lake modern loops (north/south) plus Green Lake rustic (59 sites). Pull-throughs yes. 40ft+ site count not exposed. Campendium longest camper-reported rig 33ft; reviewer reports north loop sites are longer and more level.

name: Leelanau State Park
why: Grand Traverse Lighthouse at the tip of the Leelanau peninsula, with a rustic drive-in campground on Lake Michigan.

name: Wm. Mitchell State Park
why: Modern campground on the canal between Lakes Cadillac and Mitchell, with the Carl T. Johnson Hunting and Fishing Center.

name: Fisherman's Island State Park
why: Five miles of undeveloped Lake Michigan beach and rustic drive-in sites; sandy, narrow access roads favor the pickup.

name: Hartwick Pines State Park
why: 49 acres of never-logged white pine, a logging museum and a large modern campground off I-75.

name: North Higgins Lake State Park
why: Modern campground on one of Michigan's clearest lakes, with the CCC Museum and the state's oldest tree nursery site.

name: Otsego Lake State Park
why: Small modern campground on a warm swimming lake just south of Gaylord.

name: Orchard Beach State Park
why: Bluff-top modern campground above Lake Michigan north of Manistee, with a CCC pavilion and stair access to the beach.

name: J.W. Wells State Park
why: Three miles of Green Bay shoreline and old-growth cedar with a modern campground; only 32 miles across the water from Door County but a long drive around.
rigNote: Longest site 50ft per midnrreservations mirror; electric at all sites, NO pull-throughs. 40ft+ count not exposed, but sampled site 37 is max RV 40ft on a 54ft driveway, so 40ft sites exist. Campendium longest camper-reported rig 32ft; a 30ft unit called it 'dicey' to maneuver and level, grass parking surfaces rut and get muddy.

name: Warren Dunes State Park
why: 260-foot Tower Hill dune and three miles of Lake Michigan beach, with modern and semi-modern campgrounds.
rigNote: Longest site 50ft per midnrreservations mirror (listed under the park's Mt. Randall/modern campground, 185 sites in two loops), pull-throughs yes. 40ft+ count not exposed. Listing itself warns 'units 35 feet or less will find maneuvering easier'. Campendium agrees on a 50ft max but longest camper-reported rig is a 35ft Class A. Sites are dirt/grass, no concrete pads, soft when wet.

name: Warren Woods State Park
why: One of Michigan's last virgin beech-maple forests, with a footbridge over the Galien River; day-use trails only.

name: Grand Mere State Park
why: Interdunal lakes and open dune blowouts, a well-known spring migration birding stop; day use only.

name: Indiana Dunes State Park
why: 200-foot dunes, three miles of Lake Michigan beach and the 3 Dune Challenge, with 140 all-50-amp electric sites.

name: Potato Creek State Park
why: Worster Lake with paved bike trails, a saddle barn, cabins and a big electric campground with a dump station.

name: Tippecanoe River State Park
why: Sandy oak savanna and restored prairie along the Tippecanoe, with electric camping, bridle trails and a canoe launch.

name: Ridgway State Park
why: Reservoir park at the foot of the San Juans with nearly 300 sites, including 50-amp full-hookup RV sites at Pa-Co-Chu-Puk.

name: Crawford State Park
why: 400-acre reservoir just north of the Black Canyon with fishing, waterskiing and both full- and electric-hookup sites.
rigNote: Campflare (cpwshop/ReserveAmerica mirror) shows 120ft max; Campsitephotos gives Iron Creek driveways ranging 45-120ft across 45 sites (38 with electric). Clear Fork has 21 sites (12 full hookup, 3 electric, 5 tent-only) with no published lengths. CPW's own page states no length limit. cpwshop.com blocks direct fetch (queue-it), so no first-party per-site table.

name: Sweitzer Lake State Park
why: Warm-water day-use lake at Delta known for boating and waterskiing with Grand Mesa and San Juan views.

name: Paonia State Park
why: Small 20-site reservoir park under the Ragged Mountains on the way to Kebler Pass.

name: Vega State Park
why: 8,000-ft wildflower meadows on the northeast shoulder of Grand Mesa, with an electric-hookup RV loop and tent-only loops.

name: Mancos State Park
why: Quiet Jackson Gulch Reservoir in ponderosa pine minutes from Mesa Verde; basic sites and yurts with no electrical hookups.

name: Lone Mesa State Park
why: 11,618-acre undeveloped elk and bear habitat above Dolores that is open only for hunting, volunteer and education programs.

name: Navajo State Park
why: "Colorado's answer to Lake Powell" on a 15,000-acre reservoir, with full-hookup RV sites at Rosa and electric sites at Carracas.
rigNote: Campflare (cpwshop mirror) shows 80ft park max. Outdoorsy's per-campground detail is more conservative: Rosa (39 full-hookup) and Carracas (41 electric) pull-through/back-in sites run 45-55ft; Tiffany 20-55ft. Either way there are plentiful 40ft+ sites. Windsurf Beach and Arboles Point are primitive and for small rigs only; cabin area limited to 20ft.

name: Lathrop State Park
why: Colorado's first state park, two lakes under the Spanish Peaks, with paved pull-through 50-amp sites at Pinon Campground.

name: Arkansas Headwaters Recreation Area
why: 152 river miles of the Arkansas — the nation's busiest whitewater run plus 102 miles of Gold Medal trout water — with basic riverside campgrounds at Ruby Mountain, Hecla Junction and Salida East.

name: Eleven Mile State Park
why: 3,405-acre high-plains reservoir at 8,600 ft famous for trophy trout and pike, with basic, walk-in, electric and lakeshore sites.
rigNote: Campflare (cpwshop mirror) and Outdoorsy both give 120ft max. Rocky Ridge is the big-rig campground - parking pads 20-115ft and the only electric hookups (30amp, loops A, B, D); reservations required, no first-come RV spaces there. 326 sites across nine campgrounds including 14 backcountry walk-in sites. Access roads include mountain passes and switchbacks - drive it carefully with the coach and toad.

name: Spinney Mountain State Park
why: Day-use-only Gold Medal fishery on the South Platte prized for trophy trout and pike.

name: Mueller State Park
why: 5,100 acres of meadows and Pikes Peak granite outcrops west of Pikes Peak, with electric-hookup, tent and backcountry sites.

name: Sylvan Lake State Park
why: Wooded 42-acre mountain lake ringed by White River National Forest; year-round tent and RV camping but no individual site hookups.
rigNote: CONFLICT: Campflare (cpwshop mirror) and Outdoorsy both give 120ft max at Elk Run, with Fisherman's Paradise capped at 40ft; The Dyrt reports the campground as 40ft max. 44-57 sites total, NO individual site hookups (dump station and water spigots only), 3 ADA sites, reservation required. Big-rig caution: roughly 15 miles of winding mountainous road from Eagle, and Outdoorsy explicitly warns big rigs about the approach. Treat 120ft as the pad length, not an endorsement of the drive.

name: State Forest State Park
why: 70,000-acre park billed as the moose-viewing capital of Colorado, with electric hookups, a dump station, yurts and backcountry access under the Never Summers.
rigNote: Campflare (cpwshop mirror) shows 114ft park max; Outdoorsy breaks it down by campground - Bockman 114ft, North Michigan 65ft, Ranger Lakes 60ft (32 electric sites). Crags Campground road is steep and winding and is explicitly unsuitable for RVs/trailers. Interior park roads are dirt - big-rig hostile beyond Ranger Lakes/North Michigan. CPW page publishes no length figure.

name: Lory State Park
why: 2,591-acre foothills park above Horsetooth Reservoir with 28 miles of hiking and biking trails; camping is hike-in backcountry only.

name: Boyd Lake State Park
why: 1,700-acre water-sports lake at Loveland with 140 paved pull-through sites and 20/30/50-amp hookups.
rigNote: CPW camping page: 140 paved pull-through sites with 20/30/50amp electric, 'vehicles up to 40 feet'. Campsitephotos independently confirms 'Up to 40 feet'. Hard ceiling at exactly 40ft - a 40ft coach is at the stated limit with zero margin, and the toad would need a second-vehicle space. Entry gate clearance is 14ft 2in.

name: St. Vrain State Park
why: Chain of quiet fishing ponds beside I-25 with 87 sites and two year-round campgrounds with water and electricity.
rigNote: Campflare (cpwshop mirror) shows 45ft max; Outdoorithm independently reports site limits of 40-45ft on level concrete pads. 87 sites over eight loops - sites 1-41 electric, 42-87 full hookup, 3 ADA sites. A 40ft coach fits but with little margin; the toad needs a separate vehicle space.

name: Eldorado Canyon State Park
why: World-famous sandstone climbing canyon with over 500 technical routes; day use only and a tight canyon road.

name: Golden Gate Canyon State Park
why: 12,000 acres of montane meadow and forest with 35+ miles of trails and hookup sites plus a dump station at Reverend's Ridge.

name: Barr Lake State Park
why: Prairie reservoir and bird sanctuary with 371+ recorded species and a 9-mile shoreline loop; day use only.

name: Seminoe State Park
why: Sand dunes and granite shoreline on a 21-mile reservoir at the end of the Seminoe-Alcova Backway, with electric sites at North Red Hills.

name: Sinks Canyon State Park
why: The Popo Agie River vanishes into a limestone cavern and resurfaces in a trout-filled pool at the mouth of the Wind Rivers.

name: Fort Fred Steele State Historic Site
why: Ruins of an 1868 Union Pacific-guarding Army post on the North Platte, with river access and interpretive trails.

name: South Pass City State Historic Site
why: Restored 1867 gold-rush town of 20-plus original buildings beside the Oregon Trail's South Pass.

name: Les Mason State Park
why: Small cobble-beach swimming spot on the east shore of Whitefish Lake; day use only, 8 a.m. to 8 p.m.

name: Whitefish Lake State Park
why: Compact lakeside campground and boat launch at the edge of Whitefish, popular for swimming and water-skiing.

name: Lone Pine State Park
why: Bluff-top overlooks above Kalispell with views to Flathead Lake, the Jewel Basin and Glacier; day use only.

name: Somers Beach State Park
why: Montana's newest state park on Flathead Lake's north shore, where low water exposes a vast sandy beach; day use only.

name: Wayfarers State Park (Flathead Lake)
why: Rocky shoreline cliffs and sunset vistas at Bigfork, with 30 campsites and a boat launch on Flathead Lake.
rigNote: FWP park page states a 40ft maximum RV/trailer length. Only 30 sites total, and that count includes a shared hike-bike area with 9 tent pads, so actual RV-capable sites are few. A 40ft coach is exactly at the stated ceiling - no margin, and the towed pickup will need separate parking. One fully ADA site; bear-resistant lockers required.

name: West Shore State Park (Flathead Lake)
why: Glacially carved dolomite outcrops, 33 campsites and an ice-free deep-water boat launch on Flathead's west shore.

name: Lake Mary Ronan State Park
why: Boreal-forest campground on a kokanee, perch and bass lake west of Flathead, with seasonal electricity at individual sites.

name: Yellow Bay State Park (Flathead Lake)
why: Tiny bay in the heart of Flathead's sweet-cherry orchards; only 5 first-come tent sites, no RV camping.

name: Wild Horse Island State Park
why: 2,160-acre boat-access-only island with old-growth ponderosa, bighorn sheep and a few wild horses; day use only.

name: Big Arm State Park (Flathead Lake)
why: Mature ponderosa and juniper campground with 41 sites, three yurts and Mission Mountain views; jumping-off point for Wild Horse Island.

name: Finley Point State Park (Flathead Lake)
why: Secluded conifer campground on Flathead's south end with 18 electric RV sites, cabins and boat slips.

name: Missouri Headwaters State Park
why: The confluence where the Jefferson, Madison and Gallatin form the Missouri, and a Lewis and Clark campsite.
rigNote: Campflare (Montana ReserveAmerica mirror) shows 60ft max with pull-throughs. Only 17 single-family sites plus tipis. FWP's official page publishes no length but warns that 'all boats, trailers, rigs and motorized vehicles must fit entirely within the campsite parking-spur provided' - so the coach plus the pickup must both fit the spur or the truck needs a separate space. Montana's ReserveAmerica page would not render its site table for direct verification.

name: Madison Buffalo Jump State Park
why: Semicircular cliff used for nearly 2,000 years to stampede bison herds; day use only, reached by a gravel county road.

name: Lewis & Clark Caverns State Park
why: One of the largest limestone cavern systems in the Northwest, toured by guide May-September, with a 40-site campground and cabins.

name: Henrys Lake State Park
why: Trophy cutthroat and hybrid trout lake ringed by the Continental Divide, with 83 serviced sites including full hookups.
rigNote: Campflare (Idaho ReserveAmerica mirror) shows 50ft max, pull-throughs available. 96 single-family sites: 75 water+30amp electric, 8 full hookup 50amp, plus hike/bike sites and 3 cabins. Idaho's official park page publishes no length figure and idahostateparks.reserveamerica.com blocks automated fetch, so this is not first-party. Note the dump station was closed for the 2025/26 season.

name: Harriman State Park
why: 11,000-acre former Railroad Ranch on the Henrys Fork, legendary spring-creek fly water and trumpeter swan habitat; no campground, only yurts and cabins.

name: Thousand Springs State Park
why: Six scattered units where the Snake River Aquifer bursts out of the canyon wall (Malad Gorge, Box Canyon, Niagara Springs, Ritter Island); 50 full-hookup sites at Billingsley Creek.

name: Land of the Yankee Fork State Park
why: Interpretive center at Challis for the Custer and Bonanza ghost towns and the Yankee Fork gold dredge, plus the Challis Hot Springs campground.

name: Castle Rocks State Park
why: Granite spires and world-class sport climbing next to City of Rocks, with 37 serviced sites, equestrian sites and a yurt.

name: Three Island Crossing State Park
why: Oregon Trail ford of the Snake River with a history and education center, 82 serviced campsites and a disc golf course.

name: Fort Verde State Historic Park
why: Best-preserved 1870s-80s Indian Wars cavalry post in Arizona, with four original adobe officers' quarters furnished to period.

name: Patagonia Lake State Park
why: 265-acre lake in the Santa Rita foothills that is one of southern Arizona's premier birding spots (vermilion flycatchers, herons) plus boating and lakeside camping.

name: Sonoita Creek State Natural Area
why: Nearly 10,000 acres of riparian and upland habitat behind Patagonia Lake, designated an Important Bird Area with 106 recorded species.

name: Catalina State Park
why: Saguaro forest at the foot of the Santa Catalina Mountains with Romero Pools and Sutherland Trail hikes straight off the campground.

name: Tubac Presidio State Historic Park
why: Arizona's first state park, preserving the 1752 Spanish presidio ruins seen through an underground archaeology exhibit.

name: Dead Horse Ranch State Park
why: Cottonwood-shaded lagoons and Verde River frontage with the largest full-service campground in the Verde Valley.

name: Verde River Greenway State Natural Area
why: Protects about 1,000 acres along 6 miles of one of the desert's few free-flowing rivers, under a Fremont cottonwood-willow gallery forest.

name: Oracle State Park
why: International Dark Sky Park with the 1930s Kannally Ranch House and 15 miles of trails including a stretch of the Arizona Trail.

name: Red Rock State Park
why: 286-acre Oak Creek nature preserve below Cathedral Rock with 5 miles of quiet trails and daily guided nature and bird walks.

name: Jerome State Historic Park
why: The 1916 Douglas Mansion above the Verde Valley, now a copper-mining museum in Arizona's most famous hillside ghost town.

name: Tombstone Courthouse State Historic Park
why: The 1882 Cochise County courthouse with Earp/OK Corral exhibits and a reproduction gallows in the courtyard.

name: Lost Dutchman State Park
why: Sits directly beneath the Superstition Mountains' sheer west face, launching the Siphon Draw / Flatiron climb; official page states there are no RV size restrictions.
rigNote: Campendium lists 80ft max; longest rig actually reported 43ft; tagged big-rig / pull-thru friendly. Official azstateparks facility page states 'There are no size restrictions on RVs' but gives no number, so the 80ft figure is camper/aggregator sourced. 134-135 sites, 68 with water+30/50amp electric, paved roads and pads.

name: Slide Rock State Park
why: Natural sandstone water chute in Oak Creek Canyon on a preserved 1900s apple homestead.

name: Tonto Natural Bridge State Park
why: Believed to be the largest natural travertine bridge in the world, 183 ft high over a 400-ft tunnel.

name: Picacho Peak State Park
why: 1,500-ft spire off I-10 famous for spring wildflowers, the cable-assisted Hunter Trail, and the westernmost Civil War battle site; park states no maximum RV size (no tractor trailers).
rigNote: Campflare (AZ reservation-portal mirror) shows 105ft max; Outdoorsy reports per-site length limits of 53-109ft across the Family Campground. Campendium conflictingly lists 35ft, which looks stale - a 50ft rig is logged as having stayed. Official azstateparks facility page states no maximum size, only 'no tractor trailers allowed'; 78-85 electric sites, all access paved, back-in and pull-through. Verify the specific site length at booking.

name: Roper Lake State Park
why: Stone-lined natural hot tub and a 32-acre fishing lake under Mount Graham's sky-island escarpment.

name: Kartchner Caverns State Park
why: A living limestone cave kept secret from its 1974 discovery until 1999, with the 58-ft Kubla Khan column and a summer bat roost.

name: River Island State Park
why: Small cove-and-beach park on the Parker Strip of the Colorado River with a sandy swim beach and boat launch.

name: Buckskin Mountain State Park
why: Commands one of the best views on the 18-mile Parker Strip, with riverside sites, mountain trails and 15 full-sewer spots.

name: Riordan Mansion State Historic Park
why: 1904 Arts-and-Crafts duplex log mansion in Flagstaff designed by Charles Whittlesey, with original Stickley furnishings.

name: Cattail Cove State Park
why: Two white-sand beaches on Lake Havasu with 139 hookup sites plus boat-in shoreline campsites.

name: Yuma Territorial Prison State Historic Park
why: Arizona Territory's first prison (1876-1909) above the Colorado River, with original strap-iron cells and the dark cell.

name: Alamo Lake State Park
why: Remote bass-fishing lake on the Bill Williams River with some of the darkest night skies in Arizona; 19 full-hookup sites with no stated RV length limit.

name: Hyde Memorial State Park
why: New Mexico's first state park, a cool 8,500-ft conifer canyon on the Ski Basin road that is Santa Fe's closest mountain escape.

name: Cerrillos Hills State Park
why: Five miles of trails through 1,100 years of turquoise and lead mining history above the Turquoise Trail village of Cerrillos.

name: Morphy Lake State Park
why: Tiny trout lake at 8,000 ft in the Sangre de Cristos reached by a rough road; official page caps RVs at 18 feet.

name: Storrie Lake State Park
why: Wind-swept high-plains lake north of Las Vegas known for windsurfing, fishing and birding, with 22 water-and-electric sites.

name: Villanueva State Park
why: Red sandstone bluffs boxing in the Pecos River beside two 1800s Spanish colonial villages; official page states a 40-ft RV maximum.

name: Fenton Lake State Park
why: Ponderosa-rimmed trout lake at 7,650 ft in the Jemez Mountains, good for fly fishing and winter ice fishing; only 5 water-and-electric sites.

name: Old Las Vegas Mormon Fort State Historic Park
why: The 1855 adobe remnant of the first permanent non-native settlement in the Las Vegas Valley, built at the valley's original spring.

name: Ice Age Fossils State Park
why: Nevada's newest park, protecting the Tule Springs 'Big Dig' beds where Columbian mammoths, dire wolves and ground sloths were excavated.

name: Spring Mountain Ranch State Park
why: Green spring-fed ranch under the Wilson Cliffs once owned by Vera Krupp and Howard Hughes, home to the Super Summer Theatre.

name: Cave Lake State Park
why: 32-acre reservoir at 7,300 ft in the Schell Creek Range holding brown and rainbow trout, with year-round camping and winter ice fishing.

name: Ward Charcoal Ovens State Historic Park
why: Six 30-ft beehive charcoal kilns from 1876, among the best-preserved in the country, with two large pull-through RV spaces at Willow Creek.
rigNote: CONFLICTING and unconfirmed: Campflare (ReserveNevada mirror) lists 45ft max, Outdoorsy lists 35ft. Same tier, so treat 45ft as unverified. Big-rig hostile regardless - Willow Creek has only 16 sites of which just 2 are pull-through, all camp roads and parking spurs are dirt, and access is roughly 7 miles of gravel/washboard road off US-6 (reviewers report 6-10 miles of washboard). parks.nv.gov publishes no length figure.

name: Valley of Fire State Park
why: Nevada's oldest state park: 40,000 acres of flame-red Aztec sandstone with Fire Wave, Elephant Rock and 2,000-year-old petroglyphs.

name: Quail Creek State Park
why: 600-acre reservoir with the warmest water in Utah and a mild winter climate, 15 minutes from Zion's gateway.
rigNote: Utah ReserveAmerica per-site table: longest driveway is 40ft (QU03, QU05, QU17, QU18, QU22 pull-through; QU19 back-in), QU20 is 30ft. 6 sites at 40ft, none longer. The newer QC partial-hookup sites (26 sites with power and water) show pull-through/back-in but publish no driveway length. Campflare independently reports 40ft max. A 40ft coach is at the exact ceiling; the pickup needs the second-vehicle space ($20/night).

name: Sand Hollow State Park
why: Blue reservoir ringed by red slickrock next to Sand Mountain's 6,000-acre OHV dune field - the obvious base for the tow rig.

name: Dead Horse Point State Park
why: Canyon-rim overlook 2,000 ft above a Colorado River gooseneck; two campgrounds and yurts on the mesa.

name: Kodachrome Basin State Park
why: 67 monolithic sedimentary rock spires named by a 1948 National Geographic expedition; Basin Campground has full hookups (Arch and Bryce View loops post 35-ft and 20-ft unit limits).

name: Utahraptor State Park
why: Utah's newest park at Dalton Wells, covering one of North America's largest dinosaur bone beds plus classic Moab-area 4x4 and bike terrain.

name: Snow Canyon State Park
why: Black lava flows, cinder cones and petrified white-and-red Navajo sandstone dunes in a Dark Sky-certified canyon; 38 sites with partial hookups.
rigNote: Utah ReserveAmerica per-site driveway lengths: longest is SC19 at 41ft (back-in). About 10 sites at 40ft+ - SC01-SC08, SC12, SC13 are 40ft pull-throughs (partial hookup), SC20/SC21/SC23 40ft back-ins. Remainder are 18-34ft. Group sites CTNTL1/QUAIL1 have only 35ft driveways. Effectively zero margin for a 40ft coach and no room for the toad on-site.

name: Anasazi State Park Museum
why: Excavated Coombs Site village occupied A.D. 1050-1200, one of the largest Ancestral Puebloan communities west of the Colorado, with a six-room life-size replica.

name: Red Fleet State Park
why: Three Navajo sandstone 'ships' rising from a reservoir, with a hike (or paddle) to a 200-million-year-old dinosaur trackway.

name: Coral Pink Sand Dunes State Park
why: Pink Navajo-sandstone dunes that migrate up to 50 ft a year, open to OHVs and home to the endemic Coral Pink tiger beetle; the new loop has water and electric.
rigNote: Utah ReserveAmerica per-site driveway lengths: longest 120ft (CO31 pull-through). About 19 sites at 40ft+. The partial-hookup loop CO23-CO34 is genuinely big-rig sized - 95-120ft pull-throughs plus 50-60ft back-ins (CO24, CO28). Standard sites CO04-CO22 are mostly 40ft pull-throughs. Best big-rig option in the southern Utah group.

name: Steinaker State Park
why: Warm reservoir with a sandy beach north of Vernal, an International Dark Sky Park with full-hookup, electric and dry sites.
rigNote: Utah ReserveAmerica per-site driveway lengths: longest 45ft. Roughly 11 bookable 45ft pull-throughs (ST03, ST06, ST07, ST08, ST16, ST17, ST19, ST21, ST26, ST27, ST28), several full or partial hookup. ST01HOST is also 45ft but is the host site and not bookable. Remaining sites are 25-30ft back-ins.

name: Escalante Petrified Forest State Park
why: Trails through a scatter of colorful petrified logs above Wide Hollow Reservoir, with full-hookup loops at the edge of Grand Staircase-Escalante.
rigNote: Utah ReserveAmerica per-site driveway lengths: Loop B is the big-rig loop - sites 26 and 27 at 98ft, site 25 at 78ft, site 28 at 68ft, site 29 at 53ft. Loop A is small, mostly 18-36ft with only sites 14, 17 and 24 at 40ft. 8 sites at 40ft+ total; realistically book Loop B.

name: Gunlock State Park
why: Warm red-rock reservoir famous for the short-lived spring waterfalls that spill over its slickrock spillway; 30 hookup sites.
rigNote: PerfectCamp reports sites accommodate RVs/trailers between 47 and 100ft; Campsitephotos independently states 'Campsite Vehicle Size: Up to 100 feet'. 30 sites, recently widened, with 20/30/50amp electric and water hookups, covered picnic structures, dump station. The Utah ReserveAmerica campgroundDetails page lists pull-through/back-in but does not publish the numeric driveway column, so this is mirror-sourced rather than first-party.

name: Utah Field House of Natural History State Park Museum
why: Vernal's dinosaur museum and outdoor Dinosaur Garden of life-size models, the natural indoor stop for Dinosaurland weather days.

name: Frontier Homestead State Park Museum
why: Cedar City museum of southwest Utah's iron-mission and pioneer industry, with one of the largest horse-drawn vehicle collections in the state.

name: Goblin Valley State Park
why: A Mars-like valley floor of thousands of mushroom-shaped hoodoos you can walk freely among; 14 RV spaces but no electrical hookups.

name: Green River State Park
why: Shaded cottonwood campground and boat ramp on the Green River, the put-in for Labyrinth Canyon, with a nine-hole golf course; most sites have water and electric.

name: Fremont Indian State Park and Museum
why: Clear Creek Canyon holds Utah's largest known Fremont village site and dense rock-art panels uncovered during I-70 construction; Castle Rock Campground states a 40-ft RV limit and Sam Stowe has 10 full-hookup sites.

name: Lyndon B. Johnson State Park & Historic Site
Albert & Bessie Kronkosky State Natural Area
